In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. These models have the potential to improve diagnosis and treatment outcomes in cancer care and other applications. The code used for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/UTM-CSD/tree-main.elf. Additionally, the dataset used for this research can be obtained by contacting Lucianoom@icancer.org. It will also be made available through the QUASAR-PhenoBank data sharing platform in the near future. QUASAR-PhenoBank is a resource that supports the sharing of phenotypic research data, with a focus on tumor cells and whole-slide images. The dataset used for this research consists of images derived from tumor samples that were previously characterized and annotated by pathology specialists. The images were taken from different institutions and annotated for tumor cell presence and density, with the resulting labels being used to test the performance of the trained models. The results of these tests, combined with statistical analysis, indicate that the federated approach produced models with high accuracy in detecting and classifying tumor cells within these images. Notably, the models trained using FL achieved an average loss of 0.0467 and an average accuracy of 0.953, indicating a strong correlation between the trained models and their corresponding labels. These outcomes were comparable to those of models trained with centralized data, with both approaches yielding similar ROC-AUC values and error rates. The success of this FL experiment can be attributed to several factors, including the diversity of the training datasets and the use of similar hyperparameters and models. These conditions enabled the models to converge and perform well, even in a FL environment. Based on these findings, it appears that FL has the potential to produce accurate and reliable models in tumor cell classification, among other applications. Cavity magnomechanics provides a unique setting for exploring the macroscopic quantum effects by merging magnons, phonons, and photons into a singular physical framework.  By integrating a two-dimensional magnetic material in one of the cavity mirrors, researchers have now proposed an innovative system for magnomechanics with distinct nonlinear phonon-magnon interactions, unlike conventional systems based on yttrium iron garnet which only exhibits linear coupling.  The newly designed setup yields remarkable outcomes such as stable phonon squeezing and generation of tripartite entanglements among the three modes.  The absence of additional nonlinear interactions, combined with its resilience against thermal fluctuations makes it an excellent candidate for magnomechanics and quantum-state engineering due to its inherent versatility and its ability to exploit two-dimensional magnetic interactions in an innovative manner.

Recently, a more efficient approach to controlling quadrupedal robots has been developed through reinforcement learning. This method can automatically generate skill-specific controllers without manual input, which is particularly beneficial given the complexity of tuning controllers for these robots. However, reinforcement learning often struggles to adapt to new environments, a challenge compounded by the direct action space of robot control. To overcome this obstacle, researchers previously employed intermediate spaces, like joint space, or predicted trajectory space to achieve better results. Despite these successes, these methods still require substantial pre-training to develop a basic trajectory generator. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we introduced an approach that leverages an evolutionary strategy to develop a traitor generator during reinforcement learning. This innovation enables quadrupedal robots to successfully navigate diverse terrain, including uneven and slippery surfaces, using a universal set of pre-trained policies. Our research presents a well-tested framework that can be applied to a range of complex robot tasks. The behavior of super-massive black holes in their lifetime is primarily dominated by a relatively low level of accretion well below the Eddington limit, indicating they appear as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei.  A crucial aspect of these objects is the prediction by various black hole theories and simulations that they often emit hot winds.  A recently discovered property through high-resolution spectroscopy is the presence of non-thermal velocities in the X-ray gas emitted by black holes.  We performed high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy of the low-luminosity AGN in NGC\ 7213, using data from the Chandra X-ray telescope, to investigate whether hot winds are present.  We discovered that hot winds are in fact present, as the line-of-sight emission of warm gas does not adequately account for the observed Fe XXVI K-alpha line.  We utilized the empirical warm gas model from prior studies and discovered that it cannot explain the observed Fe XXVI K-alpha line.  A wind model that includes Fe XXV and Fe XXVI yielded the best results to describe the observed emission below 1.2 keV.  We determined that hot winds account for approximately 13\% of the total AGN emission below 1.2 keV, which also includes emission from gas within the galaxy.  We utilized the observed emission longward of 1.1 keV to establish that hot winds constitute at least 75\% of the total AGN emission.  We concluded that hot winds are present and account for the previously observed non-thermal velocities, as they will cause gas velocities greater than the sound speed long before they reach a distance of 100 parsecs from the black hole.  We utilized the observed emission to establish that hot winds will likely have a significant impact on the galaxy's interstellar medium.  We predicted that hot winds will likely be observed in the majority of low-luminosity AGN, based on their prevalence in the local universe.  A hot wind will likely be detected in a future observation of NGC\ 7213, using data from the International X-ray Observatory (IXO).  The IXO will have a higher sensitivity to detect winds, as its instrument will have a greater sensitivity to detect low fluxes of gas velocities less than 5000 km/s, as opposed to the current Chandra X-ray telescope, which has a limit of 10000 km/s. To restore optimal operation, this research develops a model-free method to redesign a nonlinear control system using the limited information available from each output measurement. A natural extension of the original system dynamics is assumed to exist within a predefined neighborhood. A two-step model-free reinforcement learning approach is proposed to identify this updated system dynamics from input-output data and determine an optimal linear control strategy. Convergence analysis for the proposed method is provided, and simulation results demonstrate its effectiveness. Compared to existing methods, this new approach requires fewer output sensors and less memory, making it more suitable for a wide range of real-world applications. Additionally, it offers an innovative solution to the open-ended control problem. To validate the method, numerical simulations were conducted utilizing output measurements from a nonlinear random system, achieving nearly perfect reconstruction performance after a limited number of episodes. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-abundances, indicating a rapid and homogeneous initial star formation process. A distance modulus of 18.55 mag and a precise age of 10.35 Gyr were established through theoretical modeling of the giant branch's color-magnitude diagram, complemented by a detailed spatial analysis to identify any structural distortions within the cluster. However, we discovered that the cluster's membership consisted of multiple overlapping systems. Ultimately, we determined the projected cluster radius to be 2.9', marking the third largest in the local vicinity. Additionally, we found a weak correlation between the galactic halo's core and the cluster's movement. A photometric assessment revealed possible indicators of a binary or a stellar variability system among the cluster's members, specifically a star exhibiting a 0.35 day periodic pattern. A comprehensive analysis through tomography showed that the cluster's stars follow a symmetrical distribution, debunking initial evidence of an asymmetrical arrangement. Rather, we found the galactic bulge's orientation and the cluster's movement to be aligned with the bar's plane. Lastly, a comparison of the cluster's stellar mass and the cluster's abundance of metals fell within the established bounds of the mass-metallicity relation equation. Overall, this study offers a unique, in-depth look at the cluster and its members, providing essential information that can aid in understanding the cluster's formation and movement throughout space. Remote sensing, used to monitor Earth's condition via satellite data, has significant benefits for enhancing our daily lives and living environment. The growing number of orbiting satellites leads to the publication of multiple datasets with diverse sensors and domains to support remote sensing research. This study provides an extensive review of more than 400 publicly available datasets across various applications including land use, disaster monitoring, and weather forecasting. These datasets are analyzed based on several criteria including research impact, dataset characteristics, research areas, and geographic focus. Our research indicates that land use research benefits the most from publicly available datasets, while there is a shortage of such resources in critical areas like disaster monitoring. To fill this gap, we develop EarthNets, a comprehensive repository of over 700 remote sensing datasets spanning multiple domains and providing standardized search functionality to facilitate research. Our research shows that despite the abundance of remote sensing data, many natural disasters still claim significant lives each year. The computational power of machine learning (ML) can greatly aid remote sensing research; yet, ML models often require large datasets and significant computational resources to learn and process data. The growing ML model dependency in remote sensing research poses challenges in utilizing ML models for real-world applications, particularly in areas like embedded systems and the internet of things. The incorporation of ML models in embedded systems and the internet of things has numerous practical uses, such as monitoring natural disasters, searching for missing persons, and tracking weather patterns. As such, we advocate for more research in leveraging ML models to analyze satellite data and improve our daily lives. The detailed analysis and dataset repository provided by our research can empower AI in remote sensing research, enabling novel applications and improvements in our daily life analysis. Moreover, our research demonstrates that remote sensing data can empower AI by providing a comprehensive analysis and dataset repository. The growing number of satellites and AI models will further amplify each other's benefits, ultimately improving our daily lives. Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing concern. Existing methods focusing on spatio-temporal anomalies, which are often based on roads or grids, can result in data scarcity issues and compromised detection results. This paper introduces a novel approach that tackles these challenges. An unsupervised anomaly detection framework called ReAD is proposed to identify irregularly shaped regions with arbitrary boundaries. This framework combines spatial and temporal factors and employs a dynamic partitioning method to create homogeneous regions with contiguous locations and comparable readings. An anomaly metric is calculated for each region using a divergence calculation method, allowing for the detection of irregular areas through a weighted or adaptive approach. Experimental results, involving simulated data and real-world scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed framework. Additionally, the computational efficiency of ReAD is notable, with a computational complexity of O(n log n), facilitating its practical application. The tool box incorporating ReAD is available at https://github.com/AnonDet/ReAD. Future research directions are also discussed.

This study evaluates several theoretical pion vector form factor models in an effort to determine the most suitable match for two-pion cross sections. The ultimate goal is to minimize uncertainty in calculations for two-pion contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. By incorporating a polynomial representation of the pion vector form factor, our findings confirm that the Gounaris-Sakurai (or Kühn-Santamaria) model provides the best fit to experimental data within the 1 GeV range. Furthermore, our work suggests that the Gounaris-Sakurai model yield for the two-pion contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment is likely in the range of $[2.2\times 10^{-10}, 3.8\times 10^{-10}]$ with an estimated uncertainty of $10^{-10}$ in $10^{-14}$ electrons magnetic radius. The primary sources of uncertainty arise from the pion vector form factor itself and continuum two-pion cross sections. Lastly, our pion vector form factor analysis has been made publicly available in Mathematica format. Additionally, relevant numerical data has been compiled into CSV and TXT files for easy reference. Lastly, we report that the overall two-pion contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment lies within the range of $[-16.2, -25.5]\times 10^{-14}$ with an estimated uncertainty of $[\pm 0.6, \pm 0.7]\times 10^{-14}$ in electrons magnetic radius. This range encapsulates various theoretical estimates as well as experimental data, including the most recent results from the BABar consortium. The contribution also assesses the feasibility of distinguishing between different resonance models in the pion vector form factor with the help of future muon anomalous magnetic moment measurements precision beyond the $10^{-14}$ electrons magnetic radius threshold. Lastly, our work also explores the pion vector form factor shape and its potential links to low energy pion-pion scattering and the Sigma resonance. The pion vector form factor's shape can be tested by analyzing pion-pion forward scattering, a process that may be examined through future experiments utilizing the Higgs decay to muon-lepton and muon-pion loops. Additionally, our work suggests that the pion vector form factor at low momentum transfers could be linked to the Sigma resonance and its interactions with pions, a connection that may be examined in dedicated experiments or through advanced lattice QCD simulations, especially for calculations involving long-range momentum transfers

Developing models from source code necessitates access to an abundance of labeled information. However, trained models are frequently specialized in a task-specific manner, which undermines their transferability to other tasks. This study presents novel pre-training strategies, complemented by a graph-based code representation, aiming to produce code representations applicable across a range of tasks. Our graph-based model captures crucial interconnections between code components, enabling graph neural networks to distill common properties of code. This facilitates downstream fine-tuning across a variety of applications. Our proposed framework was evaluated using real-world datasets comprising over 30 million Java functions and nearly 800,000 Python functions, where we observed distinctive characteristics within our code representations. Through benchmarking comparisons, we established that our model yields superior performance to prevailing code representation models and is more adaptable to a range of tasks. Our source code is freely accessible at https://www.robolab.ai/code/. Additionally, the generated code representations can be retrieved via our search engine at https://search.robolab.ai/. It is also worth noting that our model has led to significant advancements in four benchmark challenges (Eclipse, Java, Keras, and PyTorch) by establishing new benchmarks. We established the first-ever benchmark for the PyTorch dataset. Our results are consistent with our hypothesis, where code diversity directly affects the performance of down-stream tasks. it presents intricate problems in practice, primarily due to variability in the brightnessof stars and system instability and noise in the measurement system. Despite these challenges, the method has attracted new attention in recent years as a means to study the atmosphere without relying on existing solar irradiance records, which can be incomplete or marred by measurement inaccuracies. Researchers from different institutions have made notable advancements along various lines of investigation. This article discusses those progressions and presents the most recent results. It includes observations from the MAESTRO flight, which took place in 2019 over Antarctica, along with both laboratory and in-flight data analysis. This article provides a comprehensive assessment of the method's strengths and weaknesses, along with a new classification of the relationship between the changes in stellar brightness and the atmosphere's aerosol content. The article concludes with a discussion of potential ground-based applications of this technique. challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple

The algorithm utilizes a set of established metrics, like the zero-crossing rate, to create an unsupervised voicing classification system, and a hybrid approach based on autocorrelation is used to calculate pitch values. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration, while exhibiting enhanced robustness and reliability. Additionally, we prove that DWIFOB's convergence rate is better than that of the proximal point algorithm, with its iteration cost being only a multiple of the number of proximal iterations. When applied to certain problems, DWIFOB can generate a convergent sequence with an asymptotic convergence rate of at least 1.5, even in the presence of noise. To achieve this, we employ a dynamically weighted averaging process reminiscent of the Katkovnik method. Moreover, we derive explicit formulas for calculating the step sizes and weighted factors in DWIFOB, which are based on the eigenvalues of specific matrices. To facilitate practical usage, we provide a set of easily applicable rules for determining these parameters in a way that yields optimal performance. Finally, DWIFOB is specifically designed to be suitable for data parallelization, making it a viable option for large-scale applications. To demonstrate its potential for real-world applications, we successfully applied DWIFOB to deblurring a blurry image and achieved better results compared to the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration. The role of neural architecture search (NAS) has escalated within the deep learning community in recent years, however its full potential is constrained by most current approaches, which explore a tiny portion of the vast neural architecture search space. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes novel techniques that make NAS more efficient by decreasing both the number of possible architectures and the computational cost associated with searching for them. These advancements are grounded in the understanding that NAS is facilitated by searching for connections that capture key characteristics of desired architectures. Consequently, this research investigates new methods of searching for neural architectures based on control parameters, using property-guided synthesis which involves capturing the characteristics of target architectures through essential properties and then searching for architectures that exhibit these properties. The results show that both the size of the search space and the computational cost required to search for it can be significantly decreased. The proposed synthesis method is also shown to outperform other NAS approaches, including those that make use of reinforcement learning and transfer learning. The synthesized architectures are then demonstrated to be highly effective on challenging classification tasks, including ImageNet. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed with distinct communication properties. It employs ensemble distillation and transfers model outputs as soft labels to participating clients and a central server via a public data set. Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the public data set. We analyzed the potential for communication efficiency in Federated Distillation by evaluating the effects of weak labels, a public data set with relevant statistics, and strong labels on communication costs. The results guided the development of two new communication-efficient distillation methods: Local Knowledge Distillation and Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Clients. These innovations were evaluated in a remote learning setting with 2000 participants and showed significant improvements in communication efficiency compared to Federated Averaging, at the cost of slight performance degradation. They achieved a 10-fold reduction in communication rounds or a 4-fold reduction in communication bits per round. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Clg20/fd. Research on Federated Distillation is a promising area of study that could enhance communication efficiency in Federated Learning. It is also outperforming other alternatives such as Federated Stochastic Gradient Descent in a study that compared different FL paradigms with a remote learning application. The current research has not been formally evaluated by the FL community, but its results compare favorably with other FL models, such as FLGAs's. The performance of Federated Distillation can be improved by utilizing local knowledge and soft labels without incurring additional communication costs. The effect of using soft labels was found to increase communication efficiency, and its benefits may be more pronounced with stronger labels, which have not been thoroughly explored in the FL literature. The public data set used for knowledge distillation also has a significant impact on communication efficiency and could potentially be customized based on the available data. The application of Federated Distillation to other FL models, such as FLGAs's, using a public data set with relevant statistics of 2000 remote learning participants, demonstrates its potential for significant communication efficiency improvements while showing a less pronounced performance degradation. The results suggest that Federated Distillation can be an efficient FL paradigm that is highly dependent on the implementation details but has the potential for considerable communication bit reductions. It achieved a 4.13 fold reduction in communication bits per round by reducing the size of the public data

A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services on large networks of interconnected computers. Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying capabilities of each node to process and generate data. Focusing on service workflows with connected components, we develop an algorithm for online, distributed control of each node's decision-making processes. Our proposed Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) method aims to achieve lower overall delays and optimal data transmission rates. It combines queuing strategies and routing discipline based on topology, using network information acquired through a new discovery approach, allowing for efficient performance under uncertain conditions. We validate SDADO with analytical models and numerical simulations demonstrating reduced end-to-end delays and optimal data transmission rates. Furthermore, the system shows improved resistance to turbulence and scalability in large networks. Key findings show that under parallel workflows, the system experiences decreased delays and increased data transmission rates, achieving a stable 5% overhead in large networks and a max 10% overhead in tiny networks. Likewise, under sequential workflows, the system experiences decreased delays and increased data transmission rates, achieving a stable 15% overhead in large networks and a max 30% overhead in tiny networks. These results make SDADO an appealing solution for managing distributed computing and service provisioning in NDN-based networks. However, the system has limitations in handling irregular workflow structures. Future work could focus on expanding the algorithm to accommodate various service models and workflow patterns. Additionally, the development of an SDADO implementation based on real-world operating systems would facilitate its practical application. These steps would ensure the readiness of the proposed algorithm for distribution and use in production environments. Furthermore, the algorithm could be applied to a broader range of distributed computing and service provisioning applications. Precise estimates of these costs and benefits could be determined through a thorough cost-benefit analysis. The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through evolutionary algorithms with no regard for domain knowledge. Alternatively, some methods utilize prior information through inverse utility analysis, but they often struggle with the computational demands. This study proposes utilizing symbolic regression with embodied utility functions, leveraging knowledge about utility function structure to balance utility learning and optimization. The results demonstrate that incorporating prior knowledge significantly enhances the utility learning process, making it more efficient and robust. Furthermore, the research reveals that embodied utility functions can be applied effectively to real-world multi-objective problems, such as optimizing features for image classification and molecules for chemical properties, with significant benefits. The utility function learning approach can be scaled up for problems with higher dimensions of utility functions and is shown to be feasible for optimizing the properties of binary molecules. The developed framework, along with the corresponding tools, is made available open-source for research purposes. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/achoudhury5/Utility-Function-Learning. The utility functions used in this research can be found at https://utility-learning.github.io/. The utility learning technique is an emerging area of research and the code, functions, and data used in this study are offered to support other researchers working in this field. The authors welcome contributions from other researchers in the form of issues or pull requests. Businesses utilize issue tracking systems to keep tabs on their projects by dividing tasks into manageable issues. This documentation style fosters gradual improvement, as each issue can be reviewed, commented on, connected to related issues, and advanced through the company workflow. Well-studied platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bugzilla have received significant attention, whereas Jira, a highly-used tracking system with a wealth of accompanying information, remains underresearched. This includes an optical dipole trap formed by the intersection of two laser beams of 850 nm, creating a pattern of traps with diameters of around 2.7 micrometers per atom, which guides a probe laser of 780 nm to stimulate and collect fluorescence emitted by the atoms. This design offers a highly compact solution for forthcoming single-atom applications including single-photon emitters, quantum registers and highly sensitive sensors. It also provides a versatile platform for the development of novel atom-chip interfaces that could be adapted for various applications using Rubidium or other similar atoms. Experimental results confirming the performance of this design are also presented, including a successful trap rate of around 70 percent, with the distances between grating elements tailored to optimize this rate. This innovative concept is expected to contribute to the advancement of monolithically integrated single-atom technologies. Due to its versatility, this design can be applied to hosting a range of different atoms while also paving the way for the integration of more complex atomic systems. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta methods, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our approach successfully yielded satisfactory results for solo patients but showed promising potential for using the proposed strategy in conjunction with other therapies for dual-patient ventilation. We provide a freely available MathCAD 3.1 worksheet that facilitates reproduction of our work and enables further research on this particular ventilation strategy. Our contribution is rooted within the broader scope of research on ventilator ventilation, a critical topic that has become even more relevant during the pandemic and may continue to be crucial in the future. Moreover, our work has the potential to address various challenges in clinical therapeutics through direct optimization of patient control. Utilizing the principles of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, we introduce an innovative method to isolate the physical properties of hadronic resonances from experimental data that may be contaminated by non-physical influences. This approach is particularly relevant when dealing with data that has not been corrected for non-physical artifacts. Unlike conventional methods, our method is grounded in the resonance mass spectrum and is unaffected by factors like different fragmentation functions. To demonstrate its efficacy, we employ this method to analyze existing data on the total hadronic cross-section and determine the physical value of the $\eta'$ mass. Furthermore, we calculate the physical value of the $f_0(980)$ mass, a value that significantly differs from its current PDG value. Based on these calculations, we assert that the method can serve as a reliable tool for extracting physical properties of hadronic resonances. Additionally, we utilize this method to assess the consistency of existing data on the total hadronic cross-section at e+e- energies above the threshold for phi production. We discover that while the data is physically consistent at energies just above the threshold for phi production, it becomes non-physical at energies above the phi threshold, a phenomenon that has been observed in previous studies. To rectify the situation, we apply the method to correct the data at energies above the phi threshold, revealing that the corrected data is purely physical. Finally, we note that our method is not only applicable to the analysis of hadronic resonances but also to other topics in hadronic physics that may be contingent upon the presence of non-physical influences. To this end, we propose that the method could be employed in future evaluations of the (g-2)_mu experiment. Additionally, the method could potentially be utilized in the optimization of experiments that are contingent upon the presence of specific resonance production. In both scenarios, the modified experiment would be grounded in the physical properties of the system in question. Consequently, the simulated data would be more conducive to the discovery of rare processes. To conclude, we acknowledge that our study is primarily based on the principles of unitarity and the resonance mass spectrum, both of which may offer fresh insights into the underlying structure of hadronic resonances. To this end, we suggest that the method could be employed in forthcoming studies on the total hadronic cross-section that may be contingent upon the presence of non-physical influences. This established link allows researchers to import concepts from geometry, such as action, momentum map, and group actions, to study complexity in a more structured environment. Lastly, researchers suggest that similarity transformations could provide a pathway to address the specification problem. Overall, this paper offers significant insights into the geometric properties of complexity in conformal field theories. Using a mathematical approach that incorporates the effects of gravitational lensing, we tested the parameters of the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model by analyzing four high-precision datasets, including the Planck satellite's data on cosmic microwave background radiation, and data from the Baryon acoustic oscillations and the redshift surveys with active galaxy nuclei and the 2-degree field gravity's Lyman-$\alpha$ forest project. Although the model generally fits the data as expected, the analysis reveals that it prefers a higher power of gravitational lensing than predicted by the model itself. Additionally, the model's fit is improved when we consider spatially flat hypersurfaces as preferred by the Lyman-$\alpha$ project data, indicating that incorporating the effects of gravitational lensing is essential in determining the rest frame of dark energy. By using the parameter $S_8$, which measures the combination of the efficiency of lensing and the combination of matter and radiation, we found that the models prefer a value of $S_8 = 0.047 \pm 0.003$ at the $1\sigma$ confidence level. Notably, the preference for a higher $S_8$ is consistent with recent findings from the SNaubel SNare and BAO datasets, whereas the models' fit prefers a higher value of the combined matter density of galaxies, indicating that the impact of gravitational lensing is significant in determining the parameter $S_8$. Lastly, we explored two possible explanations for the discrepancy between the predicted and observed values of $S_8$, including a model with spatial curvature and another with gravitational lensing's non-linear effects. However, both alternatives were found to be inconsistent with the data at a $2\sigma$ confidence level. Consequently, we suggest that the preference for a higher $S_8$ could indicate that the $\Lambda$CDM model does not adequately describe the behavior of dark energy and the effects of gravitational lensing. Therefore, we propose that the preference for a higher $S_8$ should be taken into account in future surveys, particularly those including the James Webb space telescope's observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation, as its findings could significantly impact the consistency of the $\Lambda$CDM model with observed data. The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories, often employing clone-and-modify techniques that can lead to a vast amount of shared code being maintained separately. As the number of these repositories grows, so does the need for efficient maintenance operations that can be applied to multiple repositories at once, if they contain similar files. To address this need, we introduce a novel concept called meta-maintenance, which involves identifying similar files across various repositories and performing maintenance operations on them collectively. In this study, we analyze a subset of GitHub repositories containing over 10 million files and explore the feasibility of meta-maintenance by examining the distribution of identical files, factors that influence their presence, and the characteristics of these files. Our results reveal that a substantial proportion of GitHub repositories contain identical files, which can be utilized for meta-maintenance operations, and also show that certain repository characteristics could inform the application of meta-maintenance. Furthermore, our investigation of file metadata demonstrates that meta-maintenance operations are not limited to a specific stage of the software development process. To showcase the efficacy of meta-maintenance, we successfully applied it to three real-world use cases, including a reduction in the modification of frozen files, the conversion of text files from one encoding to another, and the updating of version number information. Our research provides valuable insights for those working with GitHub repositories, and sheds light on potential applications of meta-maintenance. It also identifies issues that could be further addressed in future studies, such as the challenge of accurately detecting similar files based on their content, and the possibility of different maintenance operations having varying effects on the results. Furthermore, we propose three new directions for meta-maintenance research. First, we can investigate how meta-maintenance operations impact software quality. Second, we can explore the financial benefits of applying meta-maintenance. Third, we can examine the extent to which meta-maintenance operations reflect actual changes in the software's functional requirements. By answering these questions, we can further develop the theory and practice of meta-maintenance. It is now possible to run the code in this research through two links on GitHub. It contains nine packages that can be used for replicating the results, and these results include Figures 6-9, as well as the text in this research. The replication process took about two months and required the help of three students. They first cloned the repositories containing the files for each stage of the software development process, and then applied the maintenance operations designed to test the effectiveness of meta-maintenance

The 2008 and 2009 observations of the eclipsing binary system BD And revealed valuable insights into its nature. Calculations yielded a mass ratio of 0.97 and photometric data provided further clarity on the detached system's characteristics. Data indicated a minimal temperature difference of approximately 40 K between its components, further supported by a newly updated ephemeris that showed evidence of a periodic oscillation lasting around 9.6 years, suggesting a possible attached third component. This phenomenon may have been masked by distortions caused by the binary's eclipses and close proximity to each other, as well as the pulsations of the primary star with a primary period of 1 day, categorizing the system as a Gamma Doradus variable. This new classification contributes to a growing group of such stars and further research is necessary to fully understand the anomalies in this particular system.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within a broader framework. The new results are derived from an approach simplified by Struwe in his book. This simplified method is applicable to metrics that are $W^{2-, p}$-regular, where the conjugate exponent is 2, and p is greater than or equal to 2. In addition, this approach does not rely on the analyticity of the metric, which is a crucial consideration given the nonlocal nature of the fractional curvature. Once the existence of a single, universal blow-up solution is established, the problem of identifying its structure can be addressed. The given conditions are sufficient to demonstrate the monotonicity of the energy functional and the existence of a universal blow-up solution, which is invariant under scaling. The latter property is determined based on an analysis of the properties of the Radon transform. The same technique is used to show that the first positive eigenfunction of the fractional Yamabe problem, with normalisation under scaling, is monotonically decreasing as the exponent of the curvature falls below 4. In contrast, the same eigenfunction is monotonically increasing as the exponent lies above 4. The technique is also employed to analyse an end-time blow-up solution and show that its energy diverges as the exponent approaches 4. The same approach is used to establish a discrete set of, and maximum, exponent values for the curvature, where the monotonicity of the energy functional is preserved, and a corresponding set of monotonically increasing or decreasing first positive eigenfunctions exists. Furthermore, this research is extended to the case of initial data containing multiple connected components and establishes conditions under which the maximum component becomes the dominant solution of the flow. The maximum component of the initial data is shown to evolve deterministically, and its influence on the solution is always maximised. The same property is demonstrated to occur in the case of initially cohabiting components of differing sizes, where the largest component evolves deterministically, and the second largest component interacts with it through a sum of singular measures. The same approach is used to establish conditions of differing sizes for initial data containing precisely two components, where one component is substantially larger than the other, and the smaller component evolves deterministically, and the larger component interacts with it through a sum of singular measures.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models on two real-world datasets. Moreover, MSDCR showcases promising future directions for cross-domain recommendation by showcasing the efficacy of utilizing a well-supplied domain only to augment a user's preferences, but not necessarily for making recommendations. Consequently, MSDCR has the potential to revolutionize the area of cross-domain recommendation. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/jyhirons/MSDCR. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups. Specifically, for any group G, if a subset S generates G and meets a certain subgroup criterion, then S contains a set of group generators known as an ordered generating sequence. When S consists of reflections in a Coxeter group W, this property aligns with the concept of exchange systems (ES). In the context of finite Coxeter groups (FCGs), researchers have demonstrated the existence of ordered generating sequences comprising "bad" reflections in certain forms. Notably, in Type A n ≥ 3 groups, these sequences form a generalized basis theorem. In the current research, we extend this idea to B-type Coxeter groups by proving a generalized basis theorem for subgroups with finite Coxeter reflection criterion (FCRC). Additionally, our proof methodology in its original form is applicable to finite Crisp-Larose Coxeter groups. Furthermore, our cross-pollination of idea leads to a generalized basis theorem for finite Crisp-Larose Coxeter groups via a method different from previous approaches. In the process, we establish the ordered generating sequence in the form of "up-down" ES, where up-down ES consists of subgroups generated by "up" and "down" reflections in a specific manner. In the process, we demonstrate the existence of bad elements within up-down ES, where up-down ES fails to meet the exchange system criterion despite containing these bad elements. Furthermore, we prove a generalized basis theorem for subgroups with FCRC by removing the bad elements from up-down ES, where up-down ES meets the exchange system criterion. In the process, we identify the root system's topological properties, where up-down ES corresponds to a geometric representation of the root system. In the process, we find a correspondence between the elements of up-down ES and bivectors in a root system, where up-down ES is generated by "bad" reflections in a specific form, and subsequently, we remove the bad elements from up-down ES to demonstrate the exchange system criterion. In the process, we establish the exchange system criterion for up-down ES with "bad" elements removed, where up-down ES is an ordered generating sequence in a form of reflections in a root system. These spaces are characterized by having a specific $H$-action that allows for the realization of an $H$-SLT through the use of covering maps. Our work focuses on establishing that a strong $H$-SLT space can be expressed as the union of finite covering spaces, each of which is uniquely determined by a free $H$-action. This notion leads to the idea of a weak $H$-SLT space, and we demonstrate that these two concepts are equivalent when applied to spaces with trivial fundamental groups. Moreover, we show that a weak $H$-SLT space can be formulated using a different definition that involves the use of functors from the category of covers to the category of spaces. This new definition is found to be equivalent to the initial definition of a weak $H$-SLT space. Finally, we establish a condition of properness for functors associated with these spaces and show that this condition is necessary and sufficient for a space to be a weak $H$-SLT space. By defining and differentiating between strong and weak $\pi$-SLT spaces for any group $\pi$, we expand upon the concepts of $H$-SLT spaces. Additionally, we consider examples and discuss their implications, highlighting the relationships between these concepts and actions of groups on spaces that satisfy homotopy invariance. Lastly, we propose an interesting problem for further investigation. 

Keywords: small loop transfer spaces, strong and weak $\pi$-SLT spaces, homotopy invariant actions, homotopy invariant $\pi$-SLT actions.

We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex scenarios. The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems possessing specific properties such as irregular rewards or dynamic sensitivities. To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two distinct phases - planning and imitation - to effectively tackle these control issues. The planning stage involves determining an achievable motion plan with predicted dynamics through targeted sampling within the state space. Subsequently, the imitation stage develops an action policy capable of accurately replicating the motion plan, taking into consideration realistic sensors and actuator dynamics. Through this approach, we achieve substantial improvements in solving a diverse range of control challenges, including robotic manipulation and lunar lander simulations. The implementation details for these problems are provided on our GitHub repository. The empirical results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed strategy over traditional deep reinforcement learning and even specialized techniques for specific problem domains. More importantly, our approach ensures that all interactions are two-staged, thus reducing sensitivity to hyper-parameters and improving ethical considerations. Additionally, we provide a deeper analysis of the performance comparisons with other methodologies in Appendix 1 and the relevant codes can be accessed at https://github.com/cde-nyu/Two-Staged-Deep-RL. Key concepts from our research are also highlighted in a related blog post: https://cdenyu.github.io/2022/07/25/Two-Staged-Deep-RL.html. Essential knowledge about our research can also be obtained through our interactive Jupyter notebook available at: https://cdenyu.github.io/2022/07/25/Two-Staged-Deep-RL-nb.html. Finally, thanks to Robert Paull and Justin Lee for their contributions.

This study is the second in a series focusing on the mass distribution of black holes across various sizes, spanning from the mass of stars to supermassive entities. It specifically explores the development of supermassive black holes and uses computational methods to determine their mass over cosmic time. To accomplish this, it incorporates two main processes for growing central black holes within high-redshift galaxy precursors that produce abundant star formation. These mechanisms involve the movement of smaller stellar-mass black holes towards a central area through gaseous friction, resulting in a substantial black hole seed with a mass of $10^{3-5}$ solar masses in a relatively short timeframe. Additionally, a process of gas disk accretion onto this seed black hole, similar to the standard Eddington model, allows it to grow into a supermassive black hole, achieving a mass of $10^{6-10}$ solar masses over approximately one billion years. To validate the adopted methodology, it accurately reproduces the variations in the luminosity of active galactic nuclei at different times, their relationship to the surrounding star-formation, and the overall mass of the resulting central black hole. Subsequently, it develops the mass distribution of the remaining supermassive black holes at distinct epochs via an advanced equation and compares it to observational data from human-based studies at diverse times. Throughout the various time periods, the predicted mass distribution of the remaining supermassive black holes shows little variation but does show a slight shift towards larger masses as time passes, resulting in a gentle slope that agrees with data from human-based studies. Moreover, it proposes a common distribution that can be used to model the mass distribution of the remaining supermassive black holes at distinct epochs via an advanced equation. This distribution can be used by researchers in future studies. Lastly, it estimates the total mass of all supermassive black holes that have ever formed, revealing that this estimate agrees with data from human-based studies. To accomplish this, it computes the mass distribution of the remaining supermassive black holes at distinct epochs via an advanced equation and then multiplies this distribution by the total number of galaxies in all generations via an advanced equation. Subsequently, it computes the mass distribution of the remaining supermassive black holes at distinct epochs via an advanced equation and then multiplies this distribution by the total number of galaxies in all generations via an advanced equation. This study demonstrates that a comprehensive numerical model, which includes multiple black holes of various sizes, can accurately reproduce multiple independent observations of various phenomena by accurately setting multiple independent parameters. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this period, albeit only accounting for a small fraction of total research output. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier citation and greater recognition, as well as their potential drawbacks. The discussion concludes by addressing challenging issues in modern science communication and examining the likelihood of preprints becoming the new standard in scientific publication. Ultimately, a hybrid model that integrates the advantages of preprints and published articles in reputable journals is likely to emerge as the prevailing practice in scientific communication. A comprehensive database containing key metrics and growth statistics for preprint services from 1991 to 2020 is made available for public access. The data can serve as a reference point for users and provide a foundation for further research on the topics discussed in this review. Additionally, the supplementary materials contain in-depth discussion of specific issues and more in-depth analysis of the related data and preprints. The information on preprints by field is also detailed, including graphs that show the rapid growth and growth disparities in different fields. Furthermore, the data on citation benefits for authors is also presented, including numerical data and qualitative examples. Lastly, the discussion includes potential risks and challenges to professional reputation associated with early online dissemination of research findings through preprints. This review aims to provide an objective and comprehensive summary of the rapid growth and evolution of preprints, as well as a fair assessment of their benefits and limitations, enabling readers to form their own well-informed opinions. Conversely, it is ultimately hoped that preprints will become a regular and essential practice in scientific communication. A comprehensive database containing the necessary information for each preprint service from 1991 to 2020 is included for public reference. The data can serve as a permanent resource, a benchmark, and a foundation for future research and development. The information on preprints is also shared on various social media and communication platforms for wide dissemination and distribution. The preprints data can also be utilized for training machine learning models and developing intelligent systems, as well as for advancing natural language processing and semantic web applications. In contemporary laboratory settings, meticulous research data management is crucial. Multiple available solutions are either highly tailored or require substantial modification to be effective. This paper introduces a unified solution designed specifically for data-driven investigators working individually or in small groups. Our electronic lab journal is generated automatically from experimental notes and files, subsequently displayed on a website powered by Django. By seamlessly gathering metadata, this system minimizes manual documentation for laboratory staff and prevents errors commonly associated with entering repetitive metadata manually. Moreover, due to its reliance on extensively documented open-source libraries, users can efficiently tailor the electronic lab journal software to their requirements. A downloadable source code and demonstration website are available for interested parties.

The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its deviation from affine functions. Researchers have proposed and refined hypotheses about a specific bound for this nonlinearity; Liu, Mesnager, and Chen initially proposed a general upper limit in 2017, which Carlet later supplemented with a lower bound using differential uniformity as a reference point. Our research refines this existing lower bound using straightforward methodology based on properties of APN functions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Sidon sets within elementary abelian 2-groups and presents proof of a comprehensive upper limit for a function's nonlinearity, specifically when its differential uniformity is high. Our findings also address an open question posed by Carlet. 
We begin by defining Sidon sets and identifying the possible elements of low nonlinearity in a specific subset of elements. We establish that a function with high differential uniformity cannot have a nonlinearity that exceeds a specific threshold; however, our analysis indicates that such a threshold may be too stringent when the direct sum of two cyclic codes is involved. We establish that Sidon sets with specific properties can be found within cyclic codes and present code-based solutions to the APN-Trilinear Polynomials problem for specific dimensions. We validate the existence of a single-generator Sidon set within a specific cyclic code and present comprehensive data on Sidon sets with specific and low-weight elements. We establish that a function's nonlinearity is constrained when its direct sum of two cyclic codes is used to form a linear code. We address an open question posed by Carlet by quantifying the direct sum of two cyclic codes needed to achieve a nonlinearity of at most two. We establish that Sidon sets with specific and high-weight elements can be found within cyclic codes and and present a lower bound on the nonlinearity of a function with a specific and high uniformity property. We address an open question by identifying the minimum size required for a Sidon set with specific and high-weight elements. We establish that a non-existence proof of certain APN functions can be obtained by demonstrating the non-existence of a Sidon set with specific and high-weight elements. We establish the existence of a non-linear linear code with a specific and high nonlinearity property. We address an open question by identifying the maximum size required for a Sidon set with specific and high-weight elements and demonstrate that a non-existence proof of certain APN functions can be obtained by demonstrating the non-existence of a Sidon set with specific and high-weight elements

Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them is essential for identifying complex patterns. Researchers use various methods, such as comparing real data with simulated data that adheres to a null hypothesis. Our work involves exploring the space of binary matrices that fulfill specific row and column sum constraints, which differs from previous studies that examined random matrix generation. Our findings show that binary matrix sampling is an NP-hard problem, and our experiments using projected Gibbs sampling found that using temperature schedules in sampling leads to a greater percentage of fixed-margin simulations that match the structure of the input data. As a result, researchers can apply this knowledge to improve their tests of significance by utilizing our open-source software tools. Additionally, our experiments were based on a practical application involving peer-review data, which demonstrates the potential real-world implications of our findings. 

Keywords: Binary Matrix Sampling, Fixed Margin Binary Matrices, Gibbs Sampling, Temperature Schedules, Real-world Applications.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. We present here a theory output database and a Python package that streamlines the process of PDF fitting by providing a comprehensive and unified theoretical output library, encompassing multiple processes and cross-sections, to be used in conjunction with existing PDF fitting tools. We illustrate this package's utility by demonstrating a combined fit to lattice QCD data, parton distribution functions, and inclusive electron-positron annihilation cross-section data, using the JUNO dataset as an example. We note that while the implemented processes are sufficient for the demonstrated fit, they may not cover all required processes, and we intend to enhance the package with additional processes in the future. Additionally, we plan to release the package under an open-source license, allowing it to be publicly accessible and incorporated into other projects. We anticipate that this package will be beneficial not only to PDF fitting groups but also to other research teams working on phenomenological studies. Given its potential applications, we plan to expand the package to encompass more advanced features, such as (i) incorporating more recent theoretical developments in DGLAP evolution, (ii) integrating more processes, and (iii) enabling fitting groups to fit experimental data derived from lattice QCD, XQC, or other electron-ion colliders. We aim to have the package, named `TheoryPDFFitting`, publicly available and maintained at https://theory-pdffitting.web.cern.ch, a website providing extensive documentation and explanation of the package's functionality. The study revealed that the gap between the pump's sidebands was uniformly reproduced in the microcomb's optical spectrum, yielding an unprecedented stability of line spacing, $1.6\times10^{-13}$, at 1-second intervals. Unlike traditional microcombs, which exhibit complex and irregular subcomb patterns, parametric seeding can create a precisely equidistant frequency comb spectrum. We establish that in an acylindrically hyperbolic group G, there always exists a random subgroup that is both faithful and invariant, having a probability limit of 1 as the subgroup size approaches infinity. This result applies universally to all acylindrically hyperbolic groups, and its probability tends towards a positive limit less than 1 if G has a finite generating set. This work generalizes previous research by Clade and Wise, where they found comparable subgroups in the context of right-angled Artin groups. We further demonstrate that this phenomenon has significant implications, including the existence of faithfully represented, non-ample subgroups in G, and a proof that faithfulness is a compactly many-to-one extension property for acylindrically hyperbolic groups. This proves a portion of a conjecture proposed by Clade and Wise. Additionally, our findings provide an affirmative solution to another conjecture proposed by Behrstock, Clark, and Kalkbrener. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables under rounding, and analyzes distribution propagation through the neural network's layers. We develop a novel quasi neural network model (qNTK) to capture the network's geometry, consisting of binary weight matrices and show that they converges to the standard Thompson sampling neural tangent kernel as the number of layers approaches infinity. The set of admissible entropies derived using the Ryu-Takayanagi formula forms the Holographic Entropy Cone. This stricter set of inequalities is violated once quantum corrections are introduced through the Quantum Extremal Surface prescription. The QES method serves as a refined boundary condition that remains within these constraints, even in the presence of quantum corrections. Consequently, the HEC remains non-vanishing, thereby ensuring that subadditivity, concavity, and strong subadditivity remain valid inequality constraints. Moreover, the QES approach yields cohesive, state-independent results that are consistent across different geometric ansaetze. Using the QES method, we obtain a precise, geometrically-defined expression for the cross-coupling of two CFTs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the QES method correctly recovers the ETQS result for conical defects and the QES result for shockwave states. Lastly, we abstractly define quantum extremal surfaces in spacetime and derive key inequality constraints on entropy that are necessary for this abstract definition. Additionally, we propose several open problems and potential lines of inquiry. One such possibility is that the QES method will yield the extremal surface in the bulk, even for bulk coupling terms that are non-zero. It is also suggested that the QEC's non-vanishing nature may be attributed to the absence of bulk entanglement, which could potentially be detected through the QES method. Finally, it is conjectured that the QEC will become a strictly necessary set of inequality constraints on entropy once quantum extremal surfaces are utilized to solve the Hamiltonian diagonalization problem. As such, the QEC may be seen as an inherent, quantum extremal property of entanglement that exists independently of holography. This reduces the complex set of inequality constraints on entropy to a single, geometrically-motivated inequality, which holds for general quantum systems. The key innovation of this proposal is the creation of quantum extremal surfaces through the Hamiltonian diagonalization method, which is grounded in first-principles rather than holography. As such, this approach yields results that are consistent across different holographic models and predicts results for systems that lack a geometric dual. One such system is the TFD state on a circle, for which the QEC yields sharp predictions. Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches, which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost the speed of convergence and enable the algorithm 
to bypass noisy data, directly utilizing the prior distribution without needing 
noisy measurements. In this study, we demonstrate that these stabilization 
methods can be generalized and applied to a broad family of iterative algorithms, 
not just compressed sensing. We examine their theoretical properties, such as 
convergence and optimal iterations, and evaluate their performance in a 
compressed sensing experiment. Furthermore, we investigate alternatives to 
these stabilization methods, like neural network stabilization, which can also 
improve the algorithm's performance and achieve convergence. These techniques 
have the potential to benefit a wide range of iterative algorithms.

We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

1.  A clear illustration shows how different techniques treat pixels with varying flux ratios.
2.  A concise summary presents the core characteristics of each method.
3.  A comprehensive analysis explores the effects of objects with distinct intensity patterns on co-adding techniques.
4.  A point spread function recovery test is performed using mock observations.
5.  A point spread function is derived for the SDSS i-band images through simulation.

Our primary findings are as follows:

*   The average, weighted, and minimum-median algorithms produce co-added images with well-defined point spread functions for objects without significant brightness differences and those with an brightness ratio close to 1.
*  The average, weighted, and minimum-median algorithms fail to yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions for objects with significant brightness differences.
*  The median and minimum-median algorithms perform better than the average and weighted methods in preserving the point spread function for objects without significant brightness differences.
*  The mock observations point to difficulties in recovering point spread functions from co-added images, particularly with the median and minimum-median algorithms.
*  The derived point spread function for the SDSS i-band images through simulation suggests that the true point spread functions are larger than the originally specified value of 1.5 arcseconds. 

Our study highlights the importance of object brightness ratios in co-adding algorithms and the need for future research to determine optimal techniques for a variety of scientific applications. Additionally, we identify potential areas for improvement in current PSF reconstruction methods. 

Lastly, we present our code and mock images on GitHub under the name psfcoadd. 

We believe this work will contribute to the ongoing discussion on image co-adding and point spread function recovery.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains and associated Gaussian free fields that evolve in time. Notably, in the case of evolving domains, the GEFF becomes coupled with multiple SLE in a specific order. We also present a distinct method for creating Gaussian free field-valued processes by driving SLE with the power law process on the positive reals. This method offers an alternative framework for creating the domains and associated GEFFs that appear in the conformal framework of Dubédat and the geometric framework of Gopakumar and Nag. We believe that this new method is more computationally efficient and versatile than the conformal and geometric frameworks. We demonstrate that our creation of GEFFs is linked to the conformal and geometric frameworks. Finally, we outline several open problems and potential applications involving the new geometric objects that we have introduced. These include connecting the GEFFs to conformal quantum mechanics and the TASEP model, and defining a multiple SLE version of conformal field theory. We also believe that the new geometric objects can be used to create simulations of biological membranes and to analyze them, and that the real valley geometry can be used to analyze the spreading of fire through a forest. We also believe that the first orthant geometry is related to the spreading of fire through a room. We outline these ideas in the concluding section. In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. The estimates we derive are consistent with those from similar studies on bounded domains, which used Leray's projection operator to achieve similar results for any positive time interval. Notably, our method also allows us to extend the estimates to non-periodic initial conditions in a compact domain without a boundary. We achieve this by modifying the approach and leveraging the maximum principle, along with other tools like the Fefferman-Stein vector technique. The results we obtain for the non-periodic case are a combination of our research and the findings from an earlier study by Cañedo and Mazzulini, which is currently in review. In a separate section, we demonstrate that when the equations' right-hand side has a specific form in a certain function space, we can obtain uniform estimates for the solution's maximum norm over all time, which strongly ties the solution to the initial conditions. This extension is significant as it implies that the solution's maximum norm does not significantly change over time under these specific conditions. Notably, this form is associated with the conservation of energy in the equations. In a general sense, for any positive time interval and initial conditions, we can obtain uniform estimates for the solution's maximum norm tied to the initial conditions within that interval. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes implicitly. By training a neural network to implicitly generate these shapes over time, it is possible to generate realistic sequences showing cell growth and movement without the need for ground truth labels. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the extension of a previously established dataset of migrating cells called Diverse Realistic Cellular Motion. The generated sequence comprising over 300 frames reveals cells undergoing rapid changes with high diversity in shape. Our approach produces synthetic cell shape sequences exhibiting similar visual realism as the original dataset based on human ratings.
