This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model's efficiency was tested using a range of corrupted image datasets, and the associated numerical optimization was successfully achieved using a forward-backward type of algorithm. The corresponding documentations and source codes are available for research reproduction. The proposed method has been successfully applied to achieve state-of-the-art results in image segmentation tasks, as demonstrated by the provided reproduction results. Moreover, this approach has potential applications in a wide range of research fields, including computer vision, scientific imaging, geosciences, medical imaging, and image processing. Key research outcomes include the recovery of original image values, effective segmentation of various image objects, and optimal restoration of discontinued curves. Furthermore, this approach has been successfully applied to diverse datasets, including astronomical images, color satellite images, medical image restoration, and synthetic image segmentation. The recovery of original image values corresponds to image restoration, while effective segmentation corresponds to curve evolution and disjoint curve segmentation. The optimal restoration of discontinued curves corresponds to the simultaneous segmentation of satellite image restoration and curve denoising tasks. Detailed results and source codes for these research reproduction tasks are available. A significant contribution of this approach is the simultaneous segmentation of various image objects, which is also known as multi-label curve segmentation. This involves identifying and segmenting multiple objects within digital images, a challenging task that our approach has successfully addressed. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives. Their shared goal can be accomplished through
a unified model that achieves these tasks, as demonstrated in the paper "Uncovering
the Limits in Link Prediction and Relation Extraction" published at AAAI 2021.
However, the paper also reveals that current link prediction models are not able
to surpass state-of-the-art relation extraction models in their overall performance.
To address this shortcoming, the authors propose an ensemble-based approach that
utilizes the predictions of existing link prediction models to gain an additional
performance boost in relation extraction. The proposed approach is evaluated on
three different benchmark datasets and exhibits improved results when compared
to state-of-the-art relation extraction models. Moreover, the authors provide
insightful explanations on the extent to which link prediction models can
effectively support relation extraction. The source code of their approach has
been made publicly available for reproduction of their results at
https://github.com/epicuesta/LE-ensemble. The empirical analysis conducted
by the authors suggests that present link prediction models have a fundamental
limitation in their ability to support relation extraction and that further
advancements in link prediction models are required to effectively enhance the
performance of relation extraction models. The authors hypothesize that their
approach may still be beneficial for relation extraction models that are trained
on datasets with Mentions-View-Labels data view, as well as on smaller datasets
where the training set is sufficiently large to effectively support the
identification of target entities and their corresponding relationships. On the
other hand, the authors conclude that their approach would not yield any
notable improvements in extraction models that are trained on datasets with
Entity-View-Labels data view, as well as extraction models that lack the
support of target entities through mentions. The authors further note that
additional studies are needed in order to confirm their hypothesis and to
systematically investigate the relationship between link prediction and relation
extraction. The proposed approach is comprised of an ensemble-based strategy
that incorporates the predictions of various link prediction models to gain an
additional boost in relation extraction performance. The source code of their
approach has been made publicly available for reproduction of their results at
https://github.com/epicuesta/LE-ensemble. The authors acknowledge a prior
work published at NAACL 2019 that also aimed to establish a connection
between link prediction and relation extraction, as well as to improve the
performance of each task

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species. We observed ordered magnetic patterns for both crystals at lower temperatures, with the magnetic Scattering intensity increasing as the temperature decreased. A detailed analysis of the data allowed us to refine the magnetic parameters, confirming previous theoretical calculations. Furthermore, the differences in magnetic behavior between the two crystals were linked to their distinct crystallographic properties. We propose that this distinction arises because the smaller Nd3+ ions maintain a uniform connection with the Ru1 sites, despite the larger Tb3+ ions having a varying internal magnetic field from these sites. This led to the two ruthenium species within Tb3RuO7 being in a partially disordering state, whereas within Nd3RuO7 the two species are in a state of complete ordering. We attribute this phenomenon to a critical role of the crystallographic periodic structure in the magnetic interactions and propose that this may lead to an exclusion principle for the magnetic Scattering. A general insight into the magnetic Scattering behavior also provided valuable information for further research. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, most learning-based methods still rely on expensive and problem-specific
transformations. We introduce MPAloc, an efficient multi-dimensional
representation generator using periodic activations that produces accurate
low-dimensional representations for a wide range of data. By combining this
model with existing differential and integral operators, we significantly
boost the efficiency of learning-based local functional representations. To
evaluate our method, we developed new benchmarking tests for 2D, 3D and
eventually 6D shape reconstruction, outperforming previous approaches and
achieving even better results when combined with minimal learning-based radial
basis functions. Moreover, our model's generalizability was confirmed by
successfully applying it to new and varied geometry benchmarking tests. The
full code is openly accessible at https://github.com/isl-pc/MPAloc.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation techniques with semi-supervised learning. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches. Additionally, our method exhibits unique applications in domain-adaptation settings involving time-series data and networks. The study presents a novel framework for combining adaptation and semi-supervised learning, yielding a semi-generative model that achieves better results. Crucially, this method demands no additional labelled data, thereby enhancing the current understanding of covariate-shift adaptation. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/hilairephilippe/SemiGenerativeModel. Zhiyuan Wang and Bora Onay reviewed the paper, leading to significant improvements. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Furthermore, the geometric framework facilitates the utilization of geometric structures, such as group actions, to accelerate training and improve generalization through the transfer of knowledge across related tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate that deep learning architectures with geometric structures can be linked to the geometric structures of data, thereby enhancing the task performance of deep learning systems. Lastly, we outline future research directions based on the proposed geometric model. Interestingly, the deep learning architectures that we analyzed are found to be characterized by an inherent local symmetry, whose dimensions determine the capacity of the model. Furthermore, we found that the geometric structures of deep learning systems are susceptible to dynamic variations, such as distortions, that hinder their performance, whereas transformations, such as group actions, that preserve these geometric structures can enhance their performance. In particular, we found that geometric structures, such as loops and paths, play a crucial role in deep learning architectures and that the curvature of these structures is a critical determinant of performance. Furthermore, we found that geometric structures, such as noise and distortions, are embedded within data and that geometric structures, such as templates and quantum states, can be matched or decoded to recover the original data. We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm. Consequently, this analysis facilitates the determination of the field extension's principal factorization type based on the prime factorization of $d$. Examples illustrate the applications of our considerations to both real and non-real cubic fields. Additionally, our discussion includes reflections on the computational feasibility of our approach in comparison to other methods. Our findings are particularly convenient for use in conjunction with the LMFDB. Furthermore, our findings can be extended to examine the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in higher degree number fields. However, this would require considering multiple generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Consequently, this would complicate the determination of lattice minima and potentially the principal factorization type of the field. Nevertheless, for certain fields, specifically those of degree $6$, or multi-degree $(2,2)$, or $(3,1)$, obtained through extensions of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d_1},\sqrt{d_2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ respectively, with appropriate conditions on the generators of ambiguous principal ideals, we demonstrate how to compute the lattice minima and the associated principal factorization type in a simplified manner. These results are also documented in the LMFDB. Lastly, our work includes a theoretical consideration regarding the desired properties of a function used to certify generators of ambiguous principal ideals in cubic fields and similar functions in quadratic fields, which could provide a unified approach to computing lattice minima in number fields. This may offer a computational benefit when applying Voronoi's algorithm across different fields. This could potentially lead to time savings. Moreover, we propose an additional function that could provide a unified method for determining the principal factorization type in number fields.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. To validate our approach, we successfully demonstrate detailed comparisons with exact diagonalization results for two such systems: the extended Hubbard model on a square lattice and hydroquinone peptides with nearest-neighbor electron transfer. Our calculations include accurate determinations of energy spectra, dynamic structure factors, and correlation lengths. Moreover, we show that at sufficiently low temperatures, the system exhibits a state charactized by quantum coherence without dissipation. Our findings are consistent with observations from both transport measurements and density functional theory. Ultimately, we believe that this method will contribute significantly to unraveling the intricate physics underlying various electron correlation phenomena. Additionally, we have open-sourced our code, allowing other researchers to access and utilize our implementation. Available at https://github.com/lgrtj/mcpnn_signfold. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today. Future research should prioritize VPPM safety and security. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. Specifically, we investigate how to distribute knowledge acquired through multilingual training effectively and identify the essential elements required for successful knowledge transfer. In addition to these findings, we develop an efficient method for increasing the model's linguistic flexibility, involving the deliberate selection of key words to facilitate knowledge integration. Our model's effectiveness is verified through zero-shot learning assessments in both source and target languages. Notably, this knowledge integration approach allows us to achieve comparable results with language models that were directly trained on German and Korean, while also outperforming a model that was only fine-tuned on German. A comparable improvement is observed with the addition of Korean to the model. Our work has been successfully replicated, and code for replicating our results has been shared publicly. A detailed analysis of the effects of different training and modeling strategies on adaptability and performance has also been provided. Our study's findings could be useful for others seeking to expand the language coverage of multilingual models. In a related contribution, we successfully adapted the BigScience model to include Siberian Turkic and various dialects of Arabic. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise determination of how a system's mass is generated. Furthermore, researchers created a diagram to represent binary system formation based on total core mass and kinetic energy ratio. This study also recorded and presented various properties of proto-stellar fragments, including formation mass, thermal to gravitational energy ratio, and kinetic energy ratio. In particular, it was discovered that a binary system's mass is directly affected by its parent core's mass and energy distribution, leading to larger masses at higher core densities. This implies that if a core collapses quickly, it may produce smaller masses, whereas more massive cores that collapse slowly will yield larger masses. Additionally, researchers found that a binary system's mass is higher when it originates from a more massive core as compared to one with similar thermal to gravitational energy but lower kinetic energy. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. These narratives are rich in subjective statements, yet can be effectively identified through qualitative and quantitative analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate how narrating these narratives alters the dynamics of online debates by introducing the RETRACE system, which reconstructs narratives from conversational threads. To establish a baseline, we assess RETRACE using human annotations and propose areas for further improvement. Ultimately, demarcating distinct narratives in online discourse enables the exploration of societal narratives, thereby facilitating more productive and informed discussions. To facilitate replication, our conference paper, along with code and dataset, is publicly available at https://papyer.io. Additionally, the PAPYER dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/papyer-io/papyer_data. and the RETRACE system at https://retrace.io.

Current approaches rely on topic modeling techniques, including Latent Dirichlet Allocation, to detect events based on words and categories, but this method has several shortcomings. Firstly, topic modeling is slow due to its computationally intensive decomposition of matrices, limiting its application to small datasets. Secondly, topic modeling struggles to accurately capture events that span multiple cities. In response to these challenges, a new approach dubbed SPATE has been proposed, featuring a novel application of collaborative topic modeling alongside a dual-machine learning technique. The latter employs deep learning algorithms and is capable of providing precise event timelines. The results of SPATE from extensive experiments on real-life Twitter datasets reveal significant improvements over existing methods in terms of accuracy and coverage. The implementation of SPATE is designed such that it can analyze approximately 30,000 tweets per hour on a single laptop. New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the utility of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information on galaxy halo bias. We developed FastBiasReconstruction, a fast and accurate method for recovering halo bias from the skew-spectrum. Based on simulations, using skew-spectra alone to analyze bispectrum amplitude leads to marginally higher noise than using traditional bispectrum tomography without cross-spectra. However, combining skew-spectra with cross-spectra yields nearly the same level of noise, but with additional information on halo bias. We discovered that using skew-spectra, halo bias can be recovered at a 50% lower noise level compared to using only cross-spectra, and with the same level of accuracy as when using bispectrum tomography. We suggest employing a hierarchical analysis, starting with skew-spectrum analysis to obtain initial bias estimates, and then using bispectrum tomography to refine these estimates, while reducing statistical noise. We found that our method allows recovering halo bias at a level of $f_{b,-2(\mu=0.5)}=(2.5\pm 0.9)\mu\mathrm{eV}^{-1}$ with a $20\%$ lower noise level than traditional bispectrum tomography. We provide the code for the FastBiasReconstruction method at https://github.com/JuliaCMB/SkewCMB. We recommend further investigation on how to best analyze the cross-spectra and skew-spectrum data set, potentially including additional reconstruction methods, to determine halo bias. We expect our analysis to hold for galaxy-matter cross-correlation measurements, and propose that similar considerations apply to galaxy angular bispectrum analysis with random noise. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. The source code for this work can be found at https://github.com/jihun-han/bnns.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the need to compress them. In natural language processing, model compression has been extensively researched, especially the application of pruning to recurrent neural networks and convolutional networks. However, work in this area with natural language models is still in its early stages. This paper delves into the most recent developments in neural language model compression and explores the use of pruning as a specific effective technique. We also introduce a novel sparse recurrent neural network architecture, SRN, which incorporates the elimination of redundant memory in order to enhance word prediction, ultimately leading to a substantial reduction in the number of retained memory units from 2048 to just 19. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that by utilizing the effective length of variables in higher layers of deep models, the majority of variables can be eliminated with little to no decrease in accuracy. We also investigate the impact of quantization on recurrent neural networks, highlighting the feasibility of applying it to position-dependent recurrent neural networks (PDRNN), a superior model that outperforms standard recurrent neural networks and dropout recurrent neural networks in accuracy and computational efficiency. PDRNN can achieve a 70% reduction in computation cost while only sacrificing 0.7% of accuracy. We also present an additional method which integrates the concepts of pruning and quantization to further compress PDRNN, resulting in a model that is 2.3 times smaller in size than the original model without any decrease in accuracy. Work on pruning and quantization of dependency trees and sequence data is also briefly reviewed. We also introduce sparsity in state for recurrent neural networks and experimental results reveal that pruning and quantization can be effectively applied to state to further compress the model, achieving a 2.3 times reduction in size without any decrease in accuracy. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We demonstrate that combining multiple loss functions using weighted averages is a viable strategy, analogous to optimizing parameters through gradient descent. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/gtaylor14/Research/tree/main/loss_functions. We hope our research will facilitate increased transparency in future deep learning studies. We also propose LossFinder, an open-source tool for automatically selecting an optimal loss function. From a theoretical perspective, we provide insights into why certain loss functions are sensitive to class distribution changes, while offering possible explanations for this phenomenon. Our research is rooted in two fundamental principles: (i) the baseline model, using the simplest loss function, should always be compared to in relation to the task at hand; and (ii) since nearly all loss functions yield comparable performance in the baseline model, any improvement is likely a result of optimising a parameter (like learning rate), rather than a meaningful advancement. We also hypothesize that certain loss functions are robust to minor class distribution alterations in specific datasets. Our research is comprised of a two-part study. Part one entails examining the impact of loss function variation across 18,000 experiments, encompassing seven datasets and twelve loss functions, to validate our hypotheses. Moreover, we propose LossFinder, an open-source tool for automatically selecting an optimal loss function. Part two involves analyzing the relationship between loss function error rates and class distribution changes via comprehensive experiments. Our research is a call to action to the deep learning community to treat loss function choice as a parameter and optimise it, rather than viewing it as a fixed constant. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, researchers have been unable to derive a strict mathematical solution. Despite this obstacle, advances in computational methods, specifically density functional theory, have enabled the partial resolution of many-body problems through the separation of electron and hole states. Building on these developments, researchers have theoretically determined the conditions under which exciton condensation occurs and have successfully applied these methods to the study of exciton condensation in $\bf TiSe_2$ compound. Results from the developed model align with experimental observations of the phase transition and suggest that exciton condensation is responsible for the emergence of superconductivity in $\bf TiSe_2$ compound at low temperatures. Furthermore, the developed theoretical framework can be used to study superconductivity in other materials. On the other hand, exciton condensation can also be expressed through the use of Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations based on the obtained density functional theory results with specific parameters such as the obtained wave function and amplitude of the phase transition. These findings suggest that the developed theoretical model is a reliable tool for predicting exciton condensation and can be used as a theoretical foundation for understanding the underlying mechanisms of the phase transition in $\bf TiSe_2$ compound. Finally, the developed model presents a new theoretical approach for describing the excitonic insulator phase, which can be applied to various materials and might have potential applications in related research. Using this model, researchers can calculate and evaluate critical parameters such as the condensation pressure and amplitude of the phase transition. Ultimately, the developed theoretical model offers a groundbreaking insight into the concept of exciton condensation and its applications in materials science. Specifically, the model presents a groundbreaking prediction that the obtained wave function of the insulating phase should strongly resemble the density of states of the normal state. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is available on GitHub.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and randomly selected songs, we found that
most hit songs tend to be musically straightforward. Furthermore, we discovered
that music has become increasingly simple over the course of the studied period. 
This shift includes significant changes in the types of songs being classified as
hits. Although song textures remained stable, there was a noticeable decrease in
the volume and complexity of songs. Our analysis suggests that success in hit parades
is associated with music that is less complex. 
We verified these findings against another dataset of songs gathered from music sharing platforms,
including MIDI files from ArvPy and audio files from MagnaTagATune. Both additional datasets
confirms previous observations about music complexity. 
These findings are significant because they discuss the underlying nature of music
as an evolving phenomenon.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across all subsets of sizes $r+1$ to $Rt$. Our aim is to analyze the long-term composition of these partitions as $R$ and $t$ approach infinity. Notably, for large enough $t$, a significant portion of new entries tends to be unique to their respective groups, which means the evolution of group dynamics is essentially individualistic under the influence of time. In particular, for each group, the likelihood that a newly joined member shares the same label as existing members converges to a non-trivial probability less than 1. In essence, this phenomenon illustrates that success in gaining labels is relative and dependent on time. In the context of independent and identically distributed label assignments, the probability that a new member gains a label different from all existing members tends to zero over time. In contrast, our theoretical framework reveals that the probability of gaining a label distinct from all existing members among the first $R$ members tends to a positive number less than 1 as time approaches infinity. In the context of process $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$, this phenomenon is referred to as the "sample size effect." Our analysis also shows that the probability of mutual independence in labels among the first $R$ members converges to a positive number less than 1 as time approaches infinity. In addition, for each group, the frequency distribution of assigned labels is expected to be evenly dispersed, which means that different labels are equally likely to be assigned to newly joined members across all groups. Our theoretical results are consistent with empirical findings obtained from label exchange studies involving humans. Ultimately, the findings of our study suggest the validity of the individualistic group dynamics model in various real-world datasets, which can serve as a reference point for researchers undertaking label exchange studies. The R software package is available at https://github.com/junqiangyin/Label-Exchange/tree/master/LabelExchange package under the name "LabelExchange." It contains functions for generating empirical distributions and plotting survival and frequency distributions

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying computational aspects, emerging from a scenario where proofs are viewed as computations, and proofs are verified as computations with a specified property. This reformulation yields an interesting analogy between the standard and the intuitional versions, as well as provides a new perspective on the purely proof-theoretic original formulation. Furthermore, this paper defines a notion equivalent to the notion of contraction-free proof, referred to as purity, and demonstrates that it is a consequence of the harmony condition. Finally, this paper proposes and proves a new result, concerning the relationship between purity and the absence of proof contraction. This relationship is validated through a constructive interpretation in the Computational Ludics framework. Ultimately, this paper presents a constructive and computationally grounded understanding of the proof-theoretic notion of contraction-free proof. This new understanding is equivalent to the notion of purity, derived from a single requirement, the harmony condition.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive manner. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and manipulate the Earth's rotation, temperature gradients, and the shape of the rotating surface. The resulting flow patterns within this setup resemble baroclinic waves, which were the subject of both experimental and numerical studies over a broad range of the system's governing parameters. The observed similarities and differences between the laboratory model and numerical simulations will be highlighted, while also providing a framework for evaluating the performance of numerical climate models. The study's findings will serve as a benchmark for evaluating the accuracy of general circulation climate models. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that miniature-scale laboratory models can effectively inform the development and testing of theoretical climate models. The latter can then be utilized to make informed predictions about the future Earth's climate. The research also lays the groundwork for applying the benchmarking technique in other laboratory setups, such as those representing tropical atmospheric circulation and oceanic circulation phenomena. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. The proposed method leads to notable improvements in the accuracy of parameter estimates compared to the standard maximum likelihood approach. Furthermore, Bayesian estimation employing this method exhibits improved convergence and reduced correlation, thereby demonstrating the method's efficacy. A comparable benefit is observed for both types of extreme rainfall models. The Cumbria analysis is then used to develop regionalised extreme rainfall models for the entire UK, consisting of 24 regions and comprising a standard Pareto distribution. The parameters of these distributions are estimated using the'm' method, demonstrating a straightforward and efficient process. The accuracy of this estimation is subsequently evaluated through comparison with maximum likelihood estimates obtained via a two-stage process involving initial non-parametric analysis and subsequent regionalisation. The results show that the Bayesian approach via the'm' method is compatible with the two-stage maximum likelihood method for all UK regions. Notably, the Bayesian estimates exhibit a comparable level of accuracy to those obtained via the two-stage maximum likelihood method. Finally, the parameters of these regionalised models demonstrate a logical and easy to interpret structure, characterised by consistent and meaningful changes across the different regions. The proposed method thus succeeds in nearly orthogonalising the parameters, thereby facilitating efficient Bayesian estimation. The models and methods presented in this study can be employed in various applications involving extreme events and are available upon request. Additionally, the associated software and data used in this research are available at https://researchdata.gcrn.org.uk/d/57. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in the majority of cases, particularly under background shifts, but struggled with semantic shifts. We conducted experiments without pretraining to overcome the limitations of existing density estimation techniques, and found that this approach can successfully identify out-of-distribution examples without requiring large amounts of labeled data. In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics. Finally, using our model, we identified both slow and short-duration speed patterns characteristic of non-conservative and conservative forces, respectively. Interestingly, the speed distribution associated with the conservative force phenomenon exhibits a speed limit that is higher than that of the non-conservative force. Lastly, we observed that an electric current exists within a manageable speed range that could possibly be exploited in the development of molecular motors that tunnel electrically. Additionally, we successfully linked our model to a dual motor model, which connects the observed rotational speeds to an electric current. The connection between these theories and the dual motor model remains elusive without our model. Similarly, another theoretical model is available that attempts to explain this phenomenon, but we successfully demonstrated that our model is consistent with this dual motor model. Lastly, we proposed that our model, which describes the unidirectional rotation of Brownian molecular motors driven by electric currents, can serve as a general model for all molecular motors that tunnel electrically. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how similar they can be. This shows one-way transducers are inherently weaker. Furthermore, we found a class of non-regular languages that can only be recognized by one-way transducers, highlighting their capacity to capture complex patterns. In a related area, we also explored the'resynchronizability' concept, establishing a condition under which a one-way transducer can be modified to regain its ability to match input and produce output, even in complex situations. Interestingly, this condition yields an automatic generator for the language recognized by the transducer in such cases. In general, one-way resynchronizability remains a complex problem, but we identified specific circumstances where the issue becomes tractable. In particular, we found a algorithmic solution for verifying resynchronizability in deterministic, top-down one-way transducers with a limited number of states. This result opens the door for further research into complex two-way transducers with these characteristics. Nonetheless, we found a condition under which the issue becomes tractable for a specific class of complex transducers. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to $g$ and $h$, the resulting function, also a function of $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$, is a sum of their element-wise $f$-Convolutions, ultimately allowing us to reap benefits via the summation of their values. We demonstrate that under these conditions, even for a relatively broad class of functions $g$ and $h$, including those that map vectors to integers in a specific range, the $f$-Convolution can be computed in $n^{O(1)} \cdot |D|^{o(n)}$ time, a improvement over the previously fastest known algorithm with a time complexity of $n \cdot |D|^{\Omega(n)}$. We also show that this new algorithm is likely to be more efficient than brute force for $n$ to be greater than or equal to $\log_2 (2.52 |D|)$. Additionally, we present a new recursive approach for computing the $f$-Convolution Mod $k$, where two given $n$-dimensional vectors or functions $g$ and $h$ are subjected to the $\mod k$ operation after applying $\oplus_f$. We further establish that this new algorithm is efficient than brute force for $n$ to be greater than or equal to $\log_2 (2.72 |D|) \land n\geq 4$. Our results demonstrate that the composition of GJ 229B's atmosphere is primarily methane with some carbon to nitrogen ratio variation. We have found that the planet's spectral features align more closely with those of extremely low surface temperature methane-rich planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, rather than the higher temperature methane-rich atmosphere of Jupiter's moon Titan. A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail. As the most recent analysis has led to a $C\!P$-violating phase of $-0.24$ radians with a 1.16 standard deviation significance and a 0.10 ps inverse decay width difference with a 3.3 standard deviation significance, future predictions and projections are also outlined. The discussed topics include $B_{s}^{0}\to{J}/\psi\phi$ decays and the use of tag-and-project method to determine $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$. It is explained that the LHCb experiment will achieve a precision of nanopixels on this measurement, thus enabling a highly competitive test of the Standard Model's predictions. Nanopixel algorithms are discussed along with the advantages and challenges they pose. A possible means of enhancing precision through combining LHCb and Belle II data is also presented. Finally, a comparison between LHCb and ATLAS/LHCb $\phi_{s}$ measurements is shown. The combination of LHCb and ATLAS results in a 4.8 standard deviation significance of $C\!P$ violation. The precision of combined LHCb and Belle II measurements on $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ will likely reach a precision of 0.65 ps. A possibility of inferring $\phi_{s}$ through $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ differences between $B_{s}^{0}$ and $B_{d}^{0}$ decays is also examined. A potential future direction in $B_{d}^{0}$ decay research is then discussed. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, sneezing, and other respiratory activities. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we compared numerical simulations of a three-dimensional airflow system to a one-dimensional model. The one-dimensional system is based on the principles of fluid dynamics and mass conservation, whereas the three-dimensional model incorporates additional physical processes from the literature. By running numerical experiments that varied particle lifetimes and sources, we assessed the similarity between the two models. Furthermore, we analyzed the results in terms of the Cohen epidemic model's parameters, alpha and beta, which represented the ratio of large to small scales in the airflow system. The three-dimensional model appeared to be a reliable predictor of the one-dimensional model's behavior for large source sizes, with the latter providing a useful simplification for computational purposes. However, discrepancies between the two models emerged for smaller source sizes, with potential implications for disease transmission models. Ultimately, our study suggests that the one-dimensional model may underestimate the effectiveness of airborne control measures in confined spaces. Based on our findings, we provide guidelines for using well-mixed models in epidemiological modeling and public health applications, with recommendations for further research. Additionally, we provide context-specific parameter values for urban bus settings that could be useful to researchers in epidemiology and public health. The research has potential applications beyond urban buses, extending to other settings such as urban rail carriages, airports, and other confined public spaces. To facilitate further research, we make available our numerical code, 3D airflow simulations, and other data through dedicated repositories. The project involved participants from two institutions: University of Notre Dame and Indiana University's Advanced Data Science Institute. Roles and contributions were diverse. The authors contributed equally to the project. The lead author carried out numerical experiments, analyzed data, authored sections of the text, and maintained numerical code. The co-authors participated in code development, data analysis, writing, and research activities. This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes of tellurium isotopes $\^{135Te}$ and $\^{137Te}$. Specifically, we've investigated $\^{135Te}$'s $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray transition and $\^{137Te}$'s $\beta$-delayed $\beta$-plus $\beta$-minus transitions. We've also calculated the $\beta$-decay half-lives and $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray transition energies in line with current experimental findings. We've further utilized our shell-model results to develop theoretical tables and relativistic standard $\beta$-decay formulas, enabling us to evaluate transition intensities and other related quantities. We've then compared our findings with existing experimental and theoretical data, observing that our results demonstrate reasonable agreement with these sources. We've also assessed our computed transition multiplicities with respect to specific nuclear configurations, revealing that certain $\beta$-decay transitions can be accurately described through shell-model simulations, while others may be better explained using other theoretical models. Moreover, our study has addressed the problem of finding shell-model eigenstates corresponding to ground states of target and daughter nuclei via complex shell-model searches, yielding satisfactory results and a novel shell-model table for $\^{137Te}$ that may be useful for future research. We've also developed theoretical wave functions for nuclear, angular, and spectral factors involved in the $\beta$-decay process. These developments have enabled a more detailed understanding of the initial, intermediate, and final nuclear states involved, as well as the particle-like angular distribution of electrons following $\beta$-decay. We've also calculated the electron momentum distribution following $\beta$-decay and applied a phase-space model to determine the $\beta$-decay matrix elements and related quantities for $\^{135Te}$ and $\^{137Te}$. Furthermore, our study has established relationships between shell-model attributes and the initial, intermediate, and final nuclear states, as well as the particle-like angular distribution of electrons and electrons distributed according to momentum. We've also related our shell-model results to the spectral distribution of nuclear energy, $\gamma$-ray transition spectra, and electron energy distributions following $\beta$-decay, and have applied a phase-space model to determine the $\beta$-decay matrix elements and related quantities for $\^{135Te}$ and $\^{137Te}$. We've also calculated the $\beta$-decay properties of $\^{137Te}$ using two different shell-model spaces

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq programming language and could be executed in advance to verify the results. Moreover, we successfully demonstrated the application of our theoretical findings to a genuine trading platform by using an automatic proof tool to verify that results obtained through testing correspond to those predicted by our theoretical models. To facilitate this verification, we extended the Coq programming language by incorporating definitions and theorems describing standard double-sided auction matching algorithms. This extension is publicly available under open-source licensing. Structured as a verification proof in Coq, it reveals the step-by-step reasoning behind our work's overall correctness. To make this research more accessible, we have created an interactive visualization tool that showcases the meaning of our formalized theorems using standard Coq. This tool is also freely available online. To verify the soundness of our work, we performed a series of tests, called "fuzz tests," that tested our implementation of double-sided auctions across various scenarios. To further guarantee the robustness of our work, we performed another set of tests, called "property tests," that randomly generated exchange data to verify the consistency of our algorithm's output. This research was conducted in collaboration with industry partners, including Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, and UBS, under the guidance of the Formal Systems Laboratory at Stanford University. This research was facilitated by the Formal Transactions project. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity. This class also encompasses a substantial subset of patterns defined recursively using a limited set of rules. This, in turn, holds significant potential for significant advancements in related fields. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, nonlinearity, and the presence of uncertainties.  The application of Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) has gained significant prominence, yet it's mainly theoretical and doesn't effectively address the construction of informative compressed models.  We've developed an innovative approach, the Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO) method, which utilizes kernel learning to establish compressed models that incorporate both linear and nonlinear components in an optimal manner.  We demonstrate that complete dynamics can be accurately reconstructed from the DMD spectral factors, and that LANDO is capable of identifying the optimal linear and nonlinear structures, parameters, and their corresponding effectiveness.  The results of performing LANDO on diverse systems reveal its capability to improve the accuracy of the compressed models compared to using the DMD spectral factors directly.  Additionally, the study shows that LANDO is capable of removing artifacts that are often present in noisy and high-dimensional data, and that it can be applied to both partial and noisy data with the integration of a regularization term.  The effectiveness of the LANDO method is illustrated using different benchmark problems.  A Python package that includes the necessary code to reproduce the results in the study is available at https://github.com/Aerodynamics-Laboratory/lando\_python.  Future work will focus on extending the application of LANDO to the detection of instabilities and loss of stability in fluid dynamics. This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse. Our work also evaluates the feasibility of accretion-induced collapse using the latest computational models and highlights the necessity of advancing both theoretical and observational frameworks surrounding this phenomenon. Our analysis further notes that our understanding of millisecond pulsars is intricately linked with our comprehension of supernova explosions, stellar mergers, and other compact objects, emphasizing the necessity of considering all possible compact star pathways, including those born from double white neutron star systems via accretion-induced collapse. Our research ultimately lays the foundation for future surveys and observational studies aimed at further clarifying the intricate sequence of compact star evolution, including those requiring breakthroughs from forthcoming gravitational wave observatories. Furthermore, our findings stress the essentiality of additional observational data to clarify the origin and characteristics of millisecond pulsars. A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The provided analysis demonstrates that each constant of motion is linked to an accompanying energy function, which in turn enables a deeper understanding of the model's behavior and constraints the motion within certain bounds. Ultimately, the developed theory is shown to be effective in capturing key features of the model under consideration. Interestingly, the constructed constants of motion are found to be more capable of describing the model's behavior than several previously established constants of motion. Moreover, the theory is based solely on the given Lagrangian function without any additional assumptions or simplifications. Through user testing, we found that the retrieval performance can reach 40.47% accuracy in finding the exact class for the top-ranked results. Furthermore, we achieved an accuracy of 67.95% for subclass retrieval and 57.69% for real-world object retrieval using a deep model. These outcomes demonstrate that using VR sketches to retrieve 3D shapes achieves comparable results to traditional input methods. Additionally, user feedback showed that the retrieval results matched the expected outcomes based on the sketched shapes. Our code and dataset are available for research purposes. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, that addresses this information overload by selectively remembering crucial moments during navigation.
MemoNav uses a dual network configuration to assess both the objective's detectability in memories and the navigational significance of each memory.
By prioritizing informative memories, MemoNav leverages its constructed map guide to achieve superior performance compared to baseline methods that rely solely on visual guidance. Experimental results demonstrate MemoNav's effectiveness in diverse environments, including our introduced multiple-object multiple-goal benchmark challenge. MemoNav's optimized multi-objective sampling approach based on Inverse Square Law is also showcased. Code and models for this research are publicly available.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders various formalisms like conformal field theory both accessible and insightful. Ultimately, our study facilitates a deeper understanding of operator growth within more general Lie-symmetric systems. 

Additionally, we have observed some intriguing phenomena:

(i) Intrinsic differences exist between operator growth patterns exhibited by Lie-symmetric systems of various types (SU(1,1) and SU(2)). Specifically, SU(2) systems tend to possess more rapid operator growth compared to their SU(1,1) counterparts.

(ii) The information capacity of fundamental operators is found to be significantly higher in two-mode coherent states compared to their disjointed analogues (i.e., Coherent States that cannot be connected by any Lie algebra element).

(iii) A positive correlation exists between the algebraic tools employed to describe a system and the complexity of the system itself. Specifically, the complexity is found to be higher when utilizing SU(2) symmetry rather than SU(1,1) symmetry. 

These intriguing observations highlight the vast potential of probing Lie-symmetric systems through the lens of quantum information theory. By leveraging this approach, it may be possible to identify hidden symmetries in systems that do not initially appear connected to Lie symmetry. Furthermore, it allows for a data-driven examination of the characteristics of operator growth, which is a key aspect of understanding quantum systems of study. 

Lastly, it is noted that investigating quantum systems through the lens of quantum information theory can offer a fresh and data-driven perspective on the various characteristics of operator growth and it allows for a more observational, data-driven analysis of these characteristics.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s symmetry state is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$. The analysis utilizes data from a large-acceptance detector called the Time Projection Chamber, which measures the properties of the Hoyle state without directly detecting the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ component. The results of the investigation, obtained without the interference of an overlapping $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ decay, indicate that approximately 69% of the Hoyle state contains three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles. Additionally, the study reveals the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ component to be dominated by the 0s state, which is also consistent with the existing understanding of the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ system. The intermediate states in the Hoyle state decay, which are crucial for understanding the nuclear structure of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, were found to be predominantly the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ and $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$+$\alpha$ component in nearly equal proportions. The findings of the investigation provide new insights into the atomic structure of the Hoyle state. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the Time Projection Chamber can measure the properties of short-lived states consisting of weakly-interacting components without directly detecting all the particles in the decay system. The research paves the way for similar measurements in the investigation of other atomic systems. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at low strain rates, an oscillatory instability emerges when the nonlinear elastic length scale is involved. Conversely, at high strain rates, an Abbet-type splitting instability is expected, yet the transition between these instabilities in the strain rate regime has not been investigated. Through computational analysis, this work reveals that the nonlinear elastic scale plays a crucial role in determining the type of instability that occurs. When crack tips can be approximated as having a finite curvature, an oscillatory instability is more likely to occur, whereas at high strain rates, an Abbet-type splitting instability is more probable. Importantly, both types of instabilities can lead to tip splitting under certain conditions, thereby demarcating the zone between oscillatory and splitting instability. Notably, as the dissipative length scale emerges due to inertia, it is found that both types of instabilities can occur without its involvement. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that both the nonlinear elastic and dissipative length scales must be considered to accurately predict fracture instability in 2D dynamic fracture. Conversely, ignoring either of these scales can lead to inaccurate numerical results and even tip splitting. Based on these findings, this work proposes a method to predict fracture instability in both oscillatory and splitting forms. Furthermore, this study lays the groundwork for a unified computational approach that can determine the type of instability most likely to occur in both laboratory and numerical experiments, thereby facilitating an improved understanding and simulation of fracture instability in both scenarios. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW and its variants fail to significantly improve efficiency while still requiring a query time complexity of O(Qn), where Q is the query set and n the dataset size. To address this limitation, we introduce PrunedDTW-EA, an early abandoning variant allowing DTW to be skipped altogether under specific conditions, thereby achieving a query time complexity of O(1) for many instances. In experiments, PrunedDTW-EA yields considerable gains in execution time, especially when combined with existing optimizations. Notably, this approach proves particularly effective for similar profiles within the similarity search domain. To facilitate its integration into existing libraries and frameworks, we have open-sourced the code. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into when early abandoning is feasible and propose several open research avenues. Ultimately, PrunedDTW-Ea yields considerable improvements in efficiency while maintaining comparable accuracy. Keywords: DTW distance, early abandoning, pruned DTW, time series analysis, similarity search. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide extensive feedback
or ask probing questions to gauge understanding, but neither option incorporates
inquiry-based learning. To address this gap, we've developed a novel testing
environment that utilizes inquiry-based learning, where students learn through
conceptual feedback by defining and testing real-world applications of key
testing ideas. Unlike traditional tools that focus on coverage reports, our
approach prioritizes the importance of testing relevance, demonstrating a
significant understanding of testing efficacy among students. Building on the
success of prior studies, we empirically compared our inquiry-based learning
method to traditional tools, revealing that while all methods can educate, only
inquiry-based conceptual feedback effectively promotes testing relevance among
students. Notably, integrating testing environment with the widely-used Eclipse
framework further solidified the results, underscoring the potential of our
findings to shape the way testing is taught. Specifically, we found that when
inquiry-based learning was incorporated into Eclipse, the coverage and
relevance metrics demonstrated a substantial and significant improvement. Our
research contributes two valuable resources: (1) a testing environment that
integrates inquiry-based learning, and (2) a set of implemented empirical
investigations, both of which can be utilized by educators to educate students
about software testing. Furthermore, we identify key research questions that
can guide further studies in this area. Additionally, we discovered that the
testing environment, although small in size, has proven to be highly useful
for educational purposes, and that its effectiveness can be further enhanced by
utilizing inquiry-based learning. Specifically, we found that the standard
testing tools fell short in detecting issues compared to the testing
environment, particularly when it came to evaluating the relevance of testing
activities, a crucial aspect that was largely overlooked by the standard testing
tools. Notably, we found that the testing environment, which incorporates
inquiry-based learning, can increase the relevance of testing activities,
whereas the standard testing tools failed to achieve similar results. Ultimately,
our empirical investigation provided evidence that the testing environment,
built around inquiry-based learning, is a valuable educational resource that
can be successfully integrated into widely-used IDEs, including Eclipse, and
that its effectiveness can be studied through empirical methods. Furthermore,
our research demonstrated that the testing environment, which is small in size,
can serve as a legitimate training ground for software testing, and that its
integration with existing tools, such as Eclipse, can provide a more
comprehensive training experience

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to generalize or provide a clear understanding of how inputs influence outputs. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic representations but these methods typically assume a symbolic input space, which is not the case for deep neural networks. This paper introduces a new method called CELEBRATE that uses concept analysis and inductive logic programming to explain why certain samples are misclassified. Firstly, CELEBRATE identifies relevant attributes from training data and generates symbolic rules that characterize sub-spaces of the input domain. Secondly, it uses these rules to create a more detailed geometric representation of the misclassified samples. Lastly, it provides a clear symbolic explanation of each sample's classification outcome, showcasing its effectiveness on both binary and multi-class classification tasks with promising results. This method can be found at https://github.com/pierre-constant/CELEBRATE. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CELEBRATE surpasses existing methods in achieving high precision and recall, and it achieves up to 99\% accuracy in explaining misclassified samples. Notably, CELEBRATE's explanation capability extends to covering 98\% of test samples with the minority class at a computational cost comparable to standard visualizations. Crucially, the symbolic nature of CELEBRATE makes it more understandable and memorable than other forms of explanation. This research presents a novel approach to explaining why deep neural networks classify certain samples incorrectly, and it offers a pioneering solution to providing expressive explanations of DNNs' decisions through geometric and symbolic geometric analyses of input spaces. Additionally, this research addresses the transparency challenge by generating explanations that are easy to comprehend and retain, and it showcases that DNNs' state-of-the-art performance can be matched with a high level of interpretability. Lastly, the research presents a new method for analyzing and interpreting DNNs that can be applied to various fields including computer science, engineering and data analysis. This research is a significant contribution to the field of machine learning, particularly in explainable learning, and it addresses a critical real-world problem by enabling the understanding and justification of DNNs' decisions. This research can be applied to domains such as clinical decision-making, data protection, and marketing, among others. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, offering a means to overcome substrate limitations. Nevertheless, concrete proof of this process is scarce, primarily due to difficulties in differentiating it from other methods such as van der Waals epitaxy. Our study investigates the epitaxial behavior of the Heusler compound GdPtSb when deposited on a monolayer graphene/sapphire substrate. Through a combination of x-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and atomic force microscopy, the authors find that a high temperature and a low initial metal deposition lead to epitaxial growth with a in-plane rotation. However, this rotation can be minimized by increasing the initial metal deposition, resulting in a matching superlattice periodic structure. Ab initio calculations suggest that this matching arises from a common lattice structure with graphene, achieved through a combination of an in-plane and out-of-plane Sb shift. This periodic structure acts as a barrier, hindering the growth of a diamond-based superstructure that would result from a simpler epiphyseal growth mechanism. When the substrate is replaced with a diamond substrate or a hydrogen-terminated diamond substrate, the authors find that growth occurs solely through a pinhole or van der Waals epitaxy process. Through the exploration of these results, the authors offer potential ways to overcome remote epitaxy's current shortcomings, including the use of multiple metal deposition as a method to control epitaxial growth. Additionally, the authors note that van der Waals forces may play a key role in remote epitaxy, contrasting with their previous understanding of the process.
