Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Notably, public awareness and policymakers' interest tend to influence one another, whereas scientists are largely influenced by their own field. Conversely, economists' interest in climate change is largely driven by policymakers' interest, suggesting a significant demographic difference in how individuals within this group respond to changing climate change interest. Finally, our analysis reveals that climate change is a non-ideological issue, as both Republican and Democratic/EU interests demonstrate similar patterns and both diverge from scientists' interests. Nonetheless, when interests do diverge, policymakers are typically prompted to engage, as seen with economists' interest and certain science journals. Ultimately, our study's findings underscore the significance of norm dynamics and how different groups interact and influence one another in shaping these norms. We propose two potential mechanisms driving these interactions: (1) norm competition and (2) norm alignment, both of which require further exploration to fully comprehend their implications. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. By choosing a cost function that aligns with the underlying data, our natural gradient method can be employed to solve complex problems and uncover hidden patterns, as demonstrated through practical applications. Additionally, our approach offers a valuable tool for clarifying the underlying physics of optimization methods. To facilitate general use, our method can be automated to identify an appropriate reference manifold based on heuristic criteria. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in multiple scenarios, showcasing improved performance and enhanced physical insights. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients. Moreover, this study examines the impact of incorporating medical images on survival time prediction, revealing that using CT scans alone decreases the predictive accuracy by 6.9%, but combining CT and clinical information yields superior results. Furthermore, this research highlights the utility of applying multimodal attention to deep learning-based models and suggests the importance of clinical information when integrating visual scans in survival time prediction. Consequently, this study establishes the potential benefits of multivariate data sources for lung cancer survival time prognosis, offering valuable insights for medical professionals and patients. The proposed model, along with associated code, can be accessed at https://github.com/BioBases/BioBases.git. Experimental results demonstrate the potential for multivariate data sources to greatly improve survival time prediction, surpassing current state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, this research sheds light on the theoretical underpinnings of multivariate data sources in machine learning and biomedical research, which can inform future studies. Based on these findings, multivariate data sources may yield more accurate results in various machine learning applications, including regression tasks. To validate this hypothesis, this study conducted rigorous experiments across different data types and prediction tasks. The research is based on 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients, providing a comprehensive dataset for comparison. The study's results demonstrate that multivariate data sources can greatly improve prediction accuracy in survival times. Specifically, integrating visual medical scans along with text-based clinical information significantly outperforms sole-text-based approaches, yielding superior results. Consequently, this research offers valuable insights for medical professionals and patients, which can be accessed at https://github.com/BioBases/BioBases.git. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification that outlines desired chat behaviors. Based on
this role specification, we establish a data-driven approach to collect relevant
dialogue data using interactive annotations. Additionally, we identify key
techniques to enhance the scalability of our chat system. We evaluate the efficacy
of our proposed method on multiple role specification types and compare our
system's performance to state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, our chat system
demonstrates a notable 24.2% higher overall satisfaction score and successfully
maintains assigned roles in over 80% of conversations. The source code for
our model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yetanotherbot/role-guided-conversational-systems.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory. To describe SGWMB, researchers employed a mathematical model based on the concept of'steps' left by individual binary black hole mergers in the gravitational wave spectrum, and developed a mathematical formula to characterize the stochastic gravitational wave memory background. Based on established estimates of binary black hole occurrences, Researchers calculated that SGWMB's amplitude is likely to be less than one millionth of the amplitude of the binary black hole gravitational wave background, and predicts that SGWMB's amplitude will be around two thousandth of the amplitude of the binary black hole gravitational wave memory background. Researchers used various mathematical techniques to analyze SGWMB and found that this background can be characterized using the concept of multifractal measures, and that its behavior in the 1/f-spectrum is an indication of the binary black hole population's mass distribution. A reliable and efficient communication system known as the signaling game and a neural-based model for causal reasoning are combined to establish a platform for natural language learning. In this learning environment, one agent plays the role of a sender who encodes complex causal relationships between text-based input and output within a neural network, while a receiver acts as a learner that interprets the signaling inputs received from the sender to reconstruct the original causal structure. The system's effectiveness is tested in a scenario where there's limited common knowledge between the sender and receiver, leading to an emergent common language that facilitates robust semantic connection between them. As a result, this joint training of signaling and causal reasoning capabilities allows the system to achieve substantial generalization beyond the training data, including the ability to synthesize new causal graphs not seen during training. Additionally, the system can easily adapt to new scenarios by adjusting the system's underlying graph structure without needing access to the original data. Our experimental findings demonstrate the system's ability to establish a reliable semantic connection in the absence of common knowledge, and we've made our code available at https://github.com/y�yingchao/Signaling-Causal-RL. Additionally, a video showcasing the system's performance can be found at https://youtu.be/8pH6R7R3MkU. [Note: The link provided is subject to change over time and may need to be rewritten if the original link becomes invalid.] Experimental evidence suggests that the system's emergent common language is significantly stronger than a comparison system that uses pre-trained vocabulary to establish a connection. We've also developed a series of challenging evaluation tasks designed to assess the system's ability to recognize causal structures in various contexts, and our results indicate that the system consistently performs at or above 80% accuracy across these tests. Furthermore, we've developed a set of dynamic signaling games that allow the system to connect with multiple agents and establish a common language among them, and our results show that the system can generalize the learned semantics to new scenarios with a much smaller memory footprint than comparable systems. Overall, our research indicates that combining signaling games with neural models of causal reasoning enables the system to establish a reliable and efficient semantic connection between agents in the absence of common knowledge, and we've made significant progress in developing a system that can learn and generalize causal structures in a natural language environment. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods. However, individual approaches that rely solely on semantic or syntactic methods have demonstrated limited success in word prediction. Semantically-based models, although highly accurate, struggle to capture contextual relationships, whereas syntactically-based models excel in word prediction but lack the depth of semantic analysis. In an attempt to rectify these shortcomings, this research combines both methods and integrates a latent semantic model to mitigate these limitations. The results show that this hybrid approach not only surpasses its predecessors but also bridges the semantic and syntactic gaps. The system designed around this model won first place in the Arabic word prediction task at the SemEval-2015 competition. The code used to develop this hybrid model is freely available for public access at https://github.com/ali12/Arabic-Word-Prediction. The dataset employed in this research can be obtained from http://semweb.mmitaq.org/index.php/word-prediction. Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have improved coverage and accuracy by learning to extract relevant items from each user session. Nonetheless, current models typically combine all items within a session and often overlook the relative ranks at which they are presented, thereby disregarding substantial contextual information. Moreover, when a user's final ranked items are identified, existing models frequently fail to distinguish between these top-ranked items, thus posing a challenge for subsequent multi-item selection tasks. To address these limitations, we present a new approach, called Rank-Aware Session-based Recommentation (RASBR), which comprises two interconnected components: Rank Encoded Memory (REM) and Ranked Candidate Selection (RCS). Firstly, REM captures the inherent ranks of items within each user session by utilizing a candidate rank embedding technique, with memory weights encoded accordingly. Subsequently, RCS reads from REM to accurately retrieve the user's preferred items at each rank, thereby enabling a comparative query mechanism to disentangle the top-ranked items and guiding the system to select the best candidates. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing benchmarks in numerous benchmarks and also surpasses Multi-Item Ranking models in comprehensive ranking accuracy. Moreover, our approach shows significant improvements in relevant real-world scenarios, such as recommending the next item to a user who has listened to an album or a movie. To foster greater research in this area, we also introduce a new ranking dataset, along with comprehensive implementation details, that can be freely accessed at: https://github.com/cm-huang/RASBR. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures. Results show satisfactory convergence with increasing mesh refinement. From our studies, we observe that fractures can substantially impact flow directions, and this effect is more pronounced for more widely spaced fractures. Also, as fractures become more abundant, their impact on flow directions diminishes. Furthermore, our research reveals that when dealing with a large number of fractures, their collective surface area must be considered to fully comprehend flow and transport in fractured networks. This requires thorough mapping of fracture boundaries to maintain spatial accuracy in simulations. By mapping fracture boundaries in this manner, we achieve satisfactory convergence with mesh refinement. This mesh-independent approach can help bridge scale gaps between fracture flow models and field-scale single-phase flow simulations. Our research provides guidance on how to simulate fracture flow models from discrete fracture models to better understand fracture impact on flow directions. This involves strategies for meshing different types of fracture networks, implementing numerical solvers, and transferring fracture information to enable accurate simulation of fracture flow models. By crossing thresholds in this manner, we achieve a deeper understanding of fracture flow models and can seamlessly transition between different scales, from fracture to matrix and back again. This helps to eliminate a common source of errors in simulations by bridging scale gaps and enabling the direct simulation of complex fracture networks. Additionally, our research demonstrates that by utilizing an adaptable and detailed approach to fracture flow models, we can facilitate decision-making in energy production by accurately assessing the impact of fractures on flow and transport in natural rock formations. This involves modeling and predicting the behavior of fractures in addition to simulating single-phase flow and transport to identify areas of concern and implement decision-making strategies accordingly. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to distribute tasks across swarm controllers; secondly, developing efficient algorithms to solve the resulting optimization problems. To address the first challenge, we introduce a hierarchy of leadership within the swarm. To resolve the second issue, we introduce a novel cost function that captures the dynamics of mid-air collisions between drones. This cost function draws from the centroid-based registration technique used in computer vision to align point clouds. To evaluate our proposed method, we conduct experiments using the uAvionics platform on a swarm of drones performing complex aerial formations. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in allowing a swarm controller to maintain the shape of a pre-defined formation while avoiding collisions between drones. Additionally, compared to existing collision avoidance methods, our approach enables better avoidance of drones in high-speed mid-air collisions. Key benefits of our controller structure include low computational complexity, low communication requirements among swarm leaders, and the ability to accommodate large swarm sizes. Furthermore, our method exhibits scalable performance, as evidenced by the successful execution of complex formations with up to 20 drones. With its low power consumption characteristics, this controller structure is suitable for use in bio-inspired swarm simulations. Consequently, this work serves as a foundational knowledge base for implementing swarm simulations based on animal migration patterns. This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial's leading coefficient, and bounds for the Seidel matrix's spectral radius. Furthermore, we obtain a lower bound for the graph's minimum cut and the spectral gap, along with upper and lower bounds for the graph's effective resistance and spectral distance. Notably, these bounds hold for all chain graphs, surpassing previously established bounds which were specific to bipartite chain graphs. We verified these bounds through theoretical analysis and supported experimental evidence. These findings contribute to our understanding of the Seidel matrix's eigenvalue spectrum and matrix spectral properties. Additionally, these results have implications in analyzing the graph's topological features. The code for verifying these findings has been publicly shared.

This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. Our study enhances the existing literature, offering novel insights into fractional stochastic control problems driven by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter greater than 0.5. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the temporal context of each sentence as editors refine articles over time. We tested our approach using a dataset of German articles and found that it outperforms other established methods in a binary classification task, achieving 85.4% accuracy in distinguishing high and low quality sentences. To facilitate our results and allow for further exploration, we made our data and code available for other languages as well. Additionally, we discovered that the distribution of editing behaviors holds unique patterns for each category of articles and can distinguish high and low quality sentences, indicating potential applications in supervised machine learning. Ultimately, we aim to employ our automated system to generate labels for articles in other languages and build a comprehensive dataset of editing behaviors worldwide. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. A novel approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allows a compact model to be trained without accessing the original network's source code or training data, by training on the original network's prediction outputs instead. This is made possible by observing that these prediction outputs contain sufficient information about the original network's behavior. Notably, this method doesn't require any changes to the original network and can be applied in settings with limited computational resources. It's also compatible with both supervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios and can be used to enhance a model's performance on a variety of tasks. This method was successfully validated on various image classification datasets, which provides evidence for the method's effectiveness. Additionally, a relevant theoretical framework was established to help understand the method's behavior. Our knowledge distillation method was compared to two relevant baselines, and we demonstrate that it outperforms these baselines by a significant margin. This training strategy was successfully applied to various neural network models, using a zero-shot training protocol that doesn't require any labeled data. Furthermore, we observe that knowledge distillation can significantly improve the compact model's robustness to adversarial attacks. This study presents a novel and feasible solution to the problem of training a black-box neural network, which was previously considered to be a challenging task. This work's source code is publicly available, and we hope that our findings will contribute to the development of more efficient and robust neural networks in the future. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs a novel, agent-to-agent imitator role to filter out less informative data. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This leads to improved inference on the causal effect of a given treatment and enhances the practical applicability of this method in various contexts. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical field is reached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin correlation length. We've thoroughly characterized the magnetic properties using neutron scattering, which allowed us to track the development of BKT correlations as well as a spin-driven magnetic transition likely induced by the driven formation of topological defects at the critical field. This behavior was confidently identified through detailed observations of the intensity distribution across different momentum planes, quasipolarized spin waves, and a specific in-plane spin wave mode that exhibits a field-dependent frequency shift in agreement with a weak anisotropic magnetic field. This system presents an appealing laboratory setting in which to study the BKT physics as well as topologically enriched magnetism that can be controlled with field. Moreover, it poses an interesting comparison with a recently reported compound [Cr(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 that displayed a magnetic transition driven by quantum fluctuations. This raises an intriguing question about the potential association between magnetism of these compounds and a new family of topological liquids. Lastly, it is also possible that the magnetic transitions in these compounds could be better explained by a model in which they are weakly coupled collections of quantum BKT phases. This possibility is based on observations of decoupled BKT phases across different layers in the materials. We have demonstrated that a laboratory magnetic field can control the coupling between layers in [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 and switch the BKT regime on or off. This raises an interesting research question about whether a similar field can also control the driver of quantum magnetism in [Cr(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 and thus switch the quantum spin liquid state on or off. We look forward to answering this question through future experiments where we'll investigate whether a small interlayer exchange can be eliminated by accurately matching the layer spacing and thus achieving a truly decoupled quantum BKT phase

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation in randomness variability resulting from continuous reading of contents from SRAM. This paper proposes an SRAM-based TRGAN architecture known as TuRaN that addresses these shortcomings by allowing time-based and activity-based SRAM content access. Furthermore, TuRaN facilitates its control through undervolting, thereby enabling SRAM to act as an SRGAN. To optimize performance, various compiler-based source code modifications can be implemented to introduce diversity in access patterns. According to our evaluation, TuRaN exhibits the highest randomness variability while demonstrating high throughput, low latency, and moderate energy consumption among comparable solutions. Example implementations of TuRaN have been successfully prototested on Digilent Adept boards. TuRaN's source code and prototypes are freely accessible for review. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Our findings empower the development of new training methods and architecture designs that directly target geometric complexity, and we use these to achieve state-of-the-art results in image classification using the CIFAR-10 dataset, surpassing the performance of the acclaimed ResNet-110 model while using significantly fewer resources. Additionally, we introduce a geometric complexity-based evaluation framework for generalization performance. Our research and tools are available at https://www.learndirect.org.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.  We conducted experiments on the Fountainebleau dataset and three separate physics datasets, evaluating various data augmentation approaches to optimize model performance.  Our findings indicate that a combination of BERT and a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy enables highly accurate automated essay grading results.  We observed that a strategy involving the removal of words not found in the BERT vocabulary yields the best outcomes, surpassing the baseline BERT model by approximately 4%.  Interestingly, this approach also slightly improved the RoBERTa model's efficacy, although only marginally.  We did not employ any topic-specific fine-tuning in our study, focusing instead on the universal applicability of our approach to new topics.  Nevertheless, we discovered that incorporating a few training samples (approximately 20) from the target domain can substantially enhance model performance, indicating a promising balance between training data and adaptability.  Our research identifies key research questions for future investigation, including the feasibility of using pre-trained models adapted to new topics and the potential of increasing model performance through more sophisticated data augmentation strategies.  Additionally, we highlight practical implications for industry leaders in automated essay grading, emphasizing the importance of data-driven approaches and collaborative research efforts to resolve this persistent problem.  Furthermore, we enable replication of our study and provide open-source code on GitHub, as well as share the model configurations and data augmentation scripts on HuggingFace and GitHub, respectively.  Moreover, we make available our BERT and RoBERTa models, as well as the Fountainebleau and physics datasets for mutual benefit. The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to the integer or half-integer part of the angular momentum. This leads to a simple derivation of the Pauli exclusion principle for fermions and the symmetry of bosons, with their corresponding wavefunction factors. The principles of parity and angular momentum also provide a means to derive the quantization of magnetic moment for any type of particle. Furthermore, this approach enables a non-relativistic explanation of the swamping of electric dipole moment by orbital angular momentum for any spin, which could be significant in understanding certain phenomena in relativistic quantum field theory. A possible connection to the parity as a fundamental concept in string theory is also suggested. Finally, the possible experimental verification of the derived quantization rules for magnetic and electric dipole moments in ultra-cold atomic condensates is considered. The idea presented here is a reversal of the conventional understanding of the spin-statistics connection, where the parity symmetry is the foundational principle. This could also be a potential tool in the search for a unified theory of matter and electricity. Lastly, the possible relationship of the spin-statistics connection with the Kramers-Hubbard pairing of electric charges is explored. A possible way to observe the magnetic moment of the condensate and the role of parity in the exchange of two bosons or fermions are also suggested. Additionally, the relationship between the wavefunction exchange statistics and the magnetic moment of the condensate is revisited. Finally, the possibility of quantizing the electric charge of the condensate is a subject of discussion. The proposed concept may offer an innovative approach to fundamental particle physics. A possible future work on this research is also a subject of discussion. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, demonstrating that Delegated RingCT outperforms RingCT with efficient transaction processing capabilities while maintaining the same level of security. Specifically, Delegated RingCT transactions are processed at a rate 3-4 times higher than RingCT, based on network load. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT exhibits superior scalability characteristics. 
Key features of Delegated RingCT include support for classified transactions, complete transaction privacy, classified transaction tracking, and compliance with Know Your Customer and Anti-Money Lauzing regulations. Additionally, Delegated RingCT promotes decentralised and private smart contract implementation. 
Compared to RingCT, Delegated RingCT accelerates transaction processing by 1) reducing computational requirements, 2) minimising communication exchange, 3) optimising protocol components and 4) introducing a transaction consolidation mechanism. 
The validity and efficiency of Delegated RingCT are substantiated through evidence and a tested implementation, which also includes an ongoing transaction processing mechanism, along with an open-source code repository and a transaction processor built on top of NeoXYgen. This demonstrates Delegated RingCT's potential for widespread adoption in cryptocurrency applications. The protocol offers significant performance improvements over RingCT, without compromising on security or functionality. 
Key innovations of Delegated RingCT include the integration of linkable ring signature schemes and non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs into a public key encryption framework, along with evidence that Delegated RingCT provides reliable classification of transactions and maintains linkability across multiple transactions. Moreover, Delegated RingCT is shown to be resilient to various forms of attacks. 
Lastly, Delegated RingCT is distinguished by its low computational requirements and fast transaction processing capabilities. 
In conclusion, Delegated RingCT offers a efficient and secure solution for supporting stealth addresses in cryptocurrencies leveraging Delegated Proof of Stake.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus. The project's data and annotation guidelines are available at https://github.com/he-ud-projects/Hebrew_UD.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to handle various types of data. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple tasks without a decline in performance and with minimal computational expenses. This method can enable cooperative modeling across diverse problem areas, encompassing not just mechanics but other fields as well. Finally, the authors integrated their continual learning method with existing deep learning approaches for enhanced plasticity predictions in 3D steel microstructures, yielding excellent agreement with reference values. This research serves as a model for applying continual learning, thereby fostering cooperative modeling within the mechanics community and beyond. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, we provide evidence that enlarging the safety area correlates positively with increased online processing requirements. Lastly, potential future improvements and extensions to this research are outlined.

We have developed a comprehensive framework for determining the minimum success rate required to successfully transform one quantum state into another using probabilistic quantum protocols. Our approach is based on evaluating the relative entropy between convex cones associated with the target and resource states. By applying this framework, we tightly bound the achievable success probabilities for converting Gaussian states and clonable states. Furthermore, our findings significantly limit previous published results on achievable success probabilities in certain resource extraction scenarios, while also revealing previously unappreciated connections between quantum entanglement, discord, and our probabilistic entropy concept. Additionally, we proved that entanglement extraction and discord extraction are not mutually achievable. Our work also includes a novel upper bound on the discord of bipartite Gaussian states, along with a method for generating a Bell-diagonal target state from a Gaussian resource state, which demonstrates that our previous lower bound on discord extraction was indeed tight. Our research offers a straightforward and efficient method for determining the probabilistic convertibility of quantum states, which could be useful for a wide range of applications. Lastly, our study illustrates that relative entropy provides a more effective tool for characterizing quantum discord compared to other measures. Existing methods are evaluated and found to yield subpar results when dealing with partial views. In addition to global symmetry, PRNet also incorporates local geometric constraints to enhance correspondence robustness. Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and feature mapping, to develop a novel RNN architecture that efficiently uses parameters and generates expressive compact representations. When applied to the challenging task of action anticipation in video, Feature Mapping RNN outperforms alternative RNN models, including those with hidden state projection, in a comparative study. By utilizing Radial Basis Function kernels to map observations to a higher-dimensional space, Feature Mapping RNN maintains the topological structure of the input data, as evidenced by its superior performance when trained with Gaussian RBF kernel-based loss functions. With a limited number of parameters, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on JHMDB-21 and UCF101-24 actions anticipation tasks. Additionally, we introduce a new, larger dataset containing precise human action start times, called JHMDB-51. Experimental results demonstrate that Feature Mapping RNN's anticipated actions align more closely with the ground truth distribution compared to other RNN models. The code and dataset are publicly available for verification. Motivation The majority of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) generate unique hidden states for each time step in a sequence, which poses a significant challenge in learning from labeled data. To address this issue, parameter-sharing RNNs, including SRNN and HRNN, have been developed to reduce the number of learnable parameters by sharing weights and hiding state projections. Nevertheless, these models often fail to capture the temporal hierarchy present in numerous tasks. Action anticipation, a task that anticipates when a specific action will occur given a video's temporal context, also presents difficulties for these models as they often fail to produce compact representations and disregard the input sequence's topological structure. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a new architecture, Feature Mapping RNN (FM-RNN), which uses Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels to map observations to a higher-dimensional space while preserving the topological structure of the input data. FM-RNN consists of an input layer with parameter-sharing hidden neurons, a feature mapping layer that uses Radial Basis Function kernels, and a pooling layer that reduces the dimensionality of the representation. When applied to the challenging task of action anticipation in video, FM-RNN has been shown to outperform a range of alternative RNN models, including those with hidden state projection, as it maintains the topological structure of the input data and efficiently uses the model's parameters. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons possess a unique deformation family and derive deformation equations for the instanton gauge field and the associated connection on the associated vector bundle. These results are analogous to those previously established for the deformation theory of instantons on nearly complex symplectic 6-manifolds. Furthermore, we prove that deformations of the canonical connection on the associated bundle preserve the isomorphism class and demonstrate that explicit deformations exist for the canonical connection if and only if the instanton is connected to a zero section on the associated bundle. We also show that deformations of the canonical connection are equivalent to reductions of the associated principal G2-bundle to the action of a subgroup isomorphic to SU(2) and that the associated Higgs bundle deforms in a specific way. These findings are complemented by a detailed analysis of the case where the nearly G2-manifold is twisted into a calibrated submanifold and the deformation theory of the twisted harmonic forms. We also construct explicit deformations of an instanton on the twisted harmonic forms space for all values of the twisted connection flux. Additionally, we prove that the space of solutions to the deformation equation depends on the first Betti number of the twisted harmonic forms space and establish the connection between the deformation theory of an instanton and the deformation theory of a connection on a bundle over a complex symplectic manifold that is twisted into a real hypersurface. We show also that the deformation theory of an instanton is equivalent to the deformation theory of a connection on a bundle over a 6-dimensional product space of two hyperbolic planes and establish the connection between the deformation theory of an instanton and the deformation theory of a connection on a bundle over a 6-dimensional hyperbolic plane. Finally, we present several open problems and conjectures. These results are presented in the form of a mathematical story complete with beginning, middle and end. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on various frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of the TPC framework. For instance, with just five normalizing flows steps, TPC achieves significant improvement over standard models on car shape classification, reducing vulnerability to known composition transformations by at least 87%. Notably, with the same level of denoising steps, TPC outperforms traditional models in both unadverted and deliberately misleading (with rotation transformation) scenarios on vehicle model classification. TPC does not hinder the performance of legitimate users and significantly limits the impact of malicious users with little increase in computational complexity. As such, TPC could be a valuable security tool for various three-dimensional models in many applications. Code is available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on uncovering the underlying time-dependent and personality-driven
forces influencing temporal knowledge graph completeness. Through extensive testing
using three evaluation metrics on three different settings, we demonstrate that
our proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Our
contributions further encompass a newly developed benchmark suited for tensor
decomposition-based models that highlights time-dependent relationships. Moreover,
we employ a novel and efficient tensor completion strategy to provide dense
completion of temporal knowledge graphs. Our implementation is available online.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory is employed to investigate the relative intensities of the ground and airborne sounds, as well as their respective frequency spectra. Furthermore, experimental evidence collected in a soundproof anechoic chamber validates the theoretical predictions, offering practical insights for practitioners working with rigid-body impact sound synthesis. It is found that ground sound can be significant, but only under specific circumstances and it is not simply a matter of increasing the intensity of the impact. Ultimately, this research provides invaluable knowledge for practitioners working with rigid-body impact sound synthesis. Since ground sound can make a substantial contribution to the overall sound produced by an impact, it should not be ignored in synthesis processes. An important consideration for achieving high-quality synthesized sounds is to ensure that the receiver can hear the sound produced by the ground, which involves achieving a certain level of sound intensity and a specific frequency relationship between the ground and air sounds. Consequently, this research offers crucial knowledge for achieving realistic and high-quality synthesized sounds from rigid-body impacts. Furthermore, the study showcases the ability of the proposed method to capture evolving clusters over time. Evaluation metrics, including traditional clustering measures with adaptations, support the method's performance. Ultimately, the study successfully benchmark the approach against alternative clustering algorithms. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle. Furthermore, Arthur's interpretation of Leibnizian concepts can be reinterpreted within this formalised framework, and when restricted to a particular case involving only locally bounded quantities, this interpretation is equivalent to Arthur's. A more general approach, based on the interdependence of geometrical concepts and their application to the calculus, is also outlined, and this is closely aligned with the reasoning and results of a modern infinitesimal approach to the calculus as developed by Robert Brmed and is equivalent to the formalised Leibnizian calculus described earlier. A comparison between this approach and that of Levey, which places the development of the calculus within a broader philosophical framework, is also made. Finally, a critical examination of the significance of comparing different notions of limit or infinitesimal, and the implications this has for our understanding of the evolution of calculus, is presented. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. We demonstrate that, in most cases, the largest time estimates also serve as upper bounds for when verdicts can be determined. However, we do identify one instance where this is not the case, thus posing a question about the general validity of this expectation. As a by-product, our monitoring reformulates the 'within' operator from MITL as a combination of 'at' and 'until' operators, thereby providing an alternative characterization for a crucial aspect of verifying real-time systems. Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency. Since the system has multiple degrees of freedom, not all frequencies provide the same level of information. Intensity interferometry, a technique that exploits the cross-correlations between different measurement frequencies, could significantly improve detection capabilities by tapping into this information. By using this method, even low-frequency measurements can greatly enhance the detectability of the system, especially when high-frequency measurements are already in use. Moreover, this technique is most effective when cross-correlating frequencies are closest to each other. Frequency spreads can be quantified by effective temperatures that emerge during the signal generation process. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing graph-mapping and graph-coloring techniques to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows for quantitative comparison of different mapping algorithms in terms of resource usage. Our compiler is based on the existing SPARTAN framework and incorporates new optimization techniques for better performance, including resource sharing and graph-coloring. Despite these optimizations, some P416 programs exceed the capabilities of our target V1Model architecture, so we developed a compiler plugin to generate simplified versions of these programs, preserving key flow control characteristics. The results show significant reductions in program size, enabling successful mapping of previously infeasible programs. The full source code is available on GitHub. For more information, visit our website at spartan-p4.net. Experimental results can be found on our GitHub page under the name 'p4-v1model'. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like momentum or velocity. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields on irregular quadrilateral meshes. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a stabilized convection projection method. Both strategies were successfully tested and validated against an analytical solution in multi-dimensional settings. Our comprehensive test cases reveal that the projected Raviart-Thomas schemes achieve higher accuracy compared to their standard counterparts. Furthermore, the projected stabilized convection projection method demonstrates exceptional robustness, particularly when transporting fields across coarser meshes. Our studies indicate that both strategies can serve as reliable and accurate methods for discretising the vector transport equation. Additionally, the projected stabilized convection projection method possesses the capacity to automatically smooth the transported field, which makes it particularly suitable for a wide range of applications. Our work also identifies potential avenues for further improving the projected stabilized convection projection method, such as incorporating more sophisticated stabilization techniques. Ultimately, the choice of method depends on specific problem requirements and the desired level of accuracy and smoothness in the numerical solution. To this end, we provide concrete guidelines and recommendations for using these methods in practice. Additionally, we provide a publicly accessible code that implements these methods on GITHub for the benefit of the broader community. Since the accuracy of transporting vector-valued fields on irregular quadrilateral meshes can be enhanced using two accurate methods, we recommend using the projected stabilized convection projection method when high spatial accuracy is crucial, and the projection method when primarily aiming for accurate field propagation. Both methods can be effectively employed for numerical simulations and are particularly suited to different application scenarios. Moreover, our research indicates that further refinements to these methods may be necessary to achieve even greater accuracy in numerical solutions. To this end, we have identified potential areas for improvement in the projection method by incorporating more stable convection projection methods. Conversely, the projected stabilized convection projection method can be refined by incorporating more stable projection methods that provide superior stability and accuracy in numerical solutions. Consequently, we recommend using the projected stabilized convection projection method due to its robustness and potential for further improvement, whereas the projection method is more suitable for high-accuracy applications. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductors and analyze a related system of equations for electron and hole densities. It has been argued that in these models, solutions converge within a certain time frame. We show that this convergence is not universally applicable and that suitable measures can serve as long-term solutions. These suitable measures hinge on the model's initial conditions and its coefficients. While the model itself yields locally non-negative and conserved quantities, we analyze a related system for the densities of electrons and holes. This reformulated system, although positively defined, lacks conservation of flux. Within a confined time period, the reformulated system's solutions exhibit bounded entropy, a characteristic that translates to non-degenerate measures as long-term solutions. Nonetheless, in general, these measures do not correspond to the model's solutions. Nonetheless, under specific time-dependent initial conditions, the reformulated system's solutions demonstrate a new form of convergence. Lastly, we establish that suitable measures serve as long-term solutions for the original electron model under particular conditions. In a related context, we show that for a first-order quasi-convex hyperbolic system with a nonlinear flux, a corresponding measure-valued solution for a scalar conservation law exhibits a distinct form of convergence. This generalization to quasi-convux systems, although a significant discovery, does not extend the model's relevance to electrons and holes. We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov-Hausdorff distance. The subsets consisting of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, and we prove that these clouds are complete with respect to the GH distance. Furthermore, we identify a specific sub-cloud that contains the compact sub-clouds, and demonstrate that its elements can serve as centers for a metric structure on the GH distance class. These properties also apply to the class of spaces with at most countably many points. Additionally, we establish that the GH distance does not induce a complete metric on the class of spaces with bounded diameters. However, we prove that the GH distance is complete with respect to spaces that can be embedded uniformly into a certain standard space. These results rely on recent findings from Borel categorical theory, as well as properties of the GH distance's continuity and upper semi-continuity. Moreover, we show that the GH distance is not a perfect metric, as there exist spaces that it distinguishes only up to a certain type of approximation. Finally, we explore relationships between GH distance, bisimulation distance, and other distances such as the nodal distance and the isometric Gromov-Hausdorff distance. These investigations lead us to conjecture that these distances are not upper semi-continuous on the class of spaces with bounded diameters. Moreover, we present an example of a space that can be approached but not reached within a certain distance by the GH distance, and demonstrate that its distances can be realized as distances between certain compact sets. These ideas are tied to research on metric structure, Gromov-Hausdorff distance, metric embedding, category theory, specific spaces such as the Cantor tree, and Borel algebra. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Importantly, our surface code decoders remained resistant to failures that could compromise accurate decoding, with their robustness further verified against scenarios involving simultaneous faulty measurements. The depth of our finding is that reinforcement learning can be a valuable tool for developing algorithms, especially in areas where direct optimization approaches may encounter issues. Ultimately, our surface code decoders are found to be faster and more adaptable than existing fast decoders, while outperforming more traditional, but slower, belief propagation decoders. Specifically, our surface code decoders are within a factor of $5.4\times10^{-5}$ of the theoretical optimal loss when dealing with random noise, and can correctly determine the code state even when confronted with up to $10\%$ circuit failure rate. Additionally, our surface code decoders are compatible with joint measurement errors and noise outside the surface code's assumed probability distribution, with their robustness further verified against scenarios involving simultaneous faulty measurements. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex models or dense networks to achieve both goals, which often incurs significant computational costs. We developed an efficient approach that utilizes low-complexity features extracted from data to simultaneously improve performance and OoD handling. These features are rich in information relevant to the task at hand and can be effectively handled by linear models when data is plentiful, or by linearizing dense models when data is limited. We underpin our approach with a comprehensive theoretical analysis that explains its efficacy. Empirical testing on popular benchmarks, encompassing image classification, language modeling, and sentence classification, demonstrates the benefits of our design. Additionally, we highlight the practical value of our method by applying it to real-world medical dataset. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/nvanhout/RFC. 

Keywords: Out-of-distribution handling, optimization, feature extraction, rich features, low-complexity models, linear models, proxy tasks.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, reliable, and affordable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). Assembled from a microcontroller, a serial temperature sensor, FLC controller, and the SLM, this system successfully recreated the optimized phase map in each iteration to effectively concentrate light at multiple points within a scattering tissue environment. As proof of concept, our system formed two focal points at 5mm apart with 93.44% fitness function precision and 92.59% image clarity in a scattering tissue medium. Additionally, our system demonstrated robustness and fast convergence with repeated formations of a single focal point at 5mm away from the SLM, achieving 97.11% precision and 95.59% image clarity after 17 iterations, and formed two focal points at 5mm apart in 124 iterations, achieving 93.55% precision and 92.66% image clarity. As a versatile, affordable solution, this iterative WMA-GA combined with SLM system holds great promise for optimizing genetic algorithms, enhancing technological capabilities, and expanding application possibilities for focus formation within scattering media. Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST) technique, which utilizes sophisticated data processing to filter out speckles and enhance images, allowing for better planet detection. To test this method further, researchers have set up a controlled testbed at the Santa cruz Extreme Adaptive optics Laboratory to analyze the effectiveness of FAST in various experimental setups. Our initial findings reveal that FAST is capable of improving image clarity even under harsh conditions and that we can rely on it to achieve better results with future large telescopes. Specifically, our results demonstrate that FAST can enhance image resolution by a factor of 2.65 with the test equipment we used, or up to 6.30 with the equipment that the Maunakea Observatory would use. Our success in successfully implementing and testing the FAST method on our testbed marks a significant milestone towards perfecting the technique. Moving forward, we will refine our experimental setup to reach resolution improvements comparable to those of the Maunakea Observatory. In particular, we will tackle two key challenges: 1) efficiently harnessing the full potential of our SLM, and 2) optimizing our algorithm's performance. We are confident that our ultimate achievement will be to develop a fast and reliable system capable of providing real-time speckle removal at the pace of 50-100 kHz, a breakthrough that would unlock vast detection capabilities for both current and future ground-based astronomical telescopes. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated to be conservative when there is a limited number of studies and it is compared favorably through simulations to other established methods such as bias reduced linearization, bias reduced sandwich, and bias reduced iterative general least squares estimators.  The proposed estimators have also been successfully applied in a re-analysis of a well-known study investigating the efficacy of anti-inflammatory treatment for rheumatoid arthritis.  All simulations, as well as the analyzed data, can be accessed via publicly available R code.

This study introduces an explicit integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the explicit nature of fluid particle interaction, direct application of finite difference or Euler methods leads to an excessively restrictive time step. When using the fluid-Particle Multi-Directional Contact Algorithm (fpMDCA), the time step is limited by the collision time, which is typically much smaller than desired. By breaking down the collision phase into distinct inner and outer loops based on the fpMDCA framework, this new algorithm enables outer loop steps to approach the collision time without precision loss. Numerous tests have shown that the novel algorithm achieves time step increments comparable to the collision time, thereby significantly enhancing simulation efficiency. Furthermore, this integration method demonstrates excellent performance in diverse flow conditions, such as dilute, moderate, and dense particle flows. For complex geometrical setups like circular cylinders and spiral channels, the algorithm's effectiveness has also been thoroughly validated. Overall, this new integration method significantly accelerates particle-resolved simulations by facilitating larger time steps while maintaining precise results. Details of the algorithm can be found in the study's supplementary documentation. Related open-source code is available at the following repository: https://github.com/STC-CFD/PhPhSims/tree/phPhSims-4.0.1.102.Original.32.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. We have found that even with a coherent broadening effect considered, which is not present in perturbative QCD, the broadening patterns obtained from different models can differ significantly. Notably, at high energies such as those reached at the LHC, the broadening patterns can be differentiated by examining the transverse momentum imbalance in central collisions. This is particularly the case when using the DGLAP model to describe parton propagation, as this leads to a distinct broadening pattern compared to incoherent broadening. We have further derived explicit expressions for transverse momentum imbalance in both central and peripheral collisions, taking into account both broadening effects and final state radiation within the color dipole approach. We have observed that at high energies such as those reached at the LHC, the transverse momentum imbalance in central collisions can be represented by a power law, whereas at lower energies such as those reached at the Tevatron, a logarithmic relationship is expected. Moreover, we have observed that even with a coherent broadening effect, the transverse momentum imbalance in central collisions can be fitted using a power law over a wide energy range. We have further extracted the values of a key energy scale for different models in the color dipole approach by fitting transverse momentum spectra in central collisions at the LHC, while taking into account both broadening effects and final state radiation. We have found that this energy scale can be fitted to approximately 2 GeV, which varies depending on the model used in the broadening calculations. We have observed that even with a coherent broadening effect, the models in the broadening calculations generate different values of this energy scale.
