This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon that can be attributed to preferential sweeping - a phenomenon where turbulent motions become aligned with the direction of falling objects. This accelerative effect is found to be more pronounced when the turbulence patterns cover a broader speed range. Additionally, it is observed that when the atmosphere's turbulence patterns display cluster structures, a preferential sweeping effect is also observed, further underscoring its importance in snow deposition dynamics. Our research lays the groundwork for a new theoretical framework that can quantify the dynamics of snow deposition. Such a framework holds broader applications, not only in snow physics but also in biological and atmospheric sciences. Furthermore, our research is poised to be a pioneering work in multiple fields, where a preferential sweeping effect has yet to be thoroughly documented. Based on our findings, high-resolution atmospheric flow modeling is needed to thoroughly understand and predict snow deposition patterns. This research reveals that without accurately capturing the rapid variations in atmospheric turbulence, snow deposition models will necessarily be incomplete. Our research implies that snow deposition that arises from conventional settling processes may be insufficient to accurately model large snowdrifts, a finding that has practical applications and implications. Finally, our research suggests that a numerical model incorporating preferential sweeping could provide a more accurate prediction of snowdrift patterns, a claim that will be tested in a follow-up study. Moreover, our research indicates that this phenomenon has yet to be thoroughly explored in atmospheric turbulence research. Based on our research findings, preferential sweeping could also impact the deposition of biological organisms, pollen, and other particles that settle from the atmosphere. Our research reveals that the effect of turbulence on settling particles is a complex phenomenon that is best captured through detailed observations of the flow patterns and settling patterns of these particles. Our research demonstrates that high-resolution imaging is essential to accurately quantify the role of turbulence in settling patterns, a finding that is critical for understanding this interaction. Finally, our research suggests that a new theoretical framework is needed to accurately model the deposition of particles that settle from the atmosphere

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates deep neural networks into the active inference framework, eliminating mental model constraints and enabling the direct utilization of sensor data within a Bayesian context. As a demonstration of the theoretical advancements, we integrated this method into a brain-inspired robot navigation system. Compared to existing reinforcement learning methods, this approach results in faster learning rates and more resilient performance, as evidenced by extensive experiments involving real-world robot navigation tasks. Furthermore, the evaluation confirmed that the developed agent adheres to principled Bayesian guidelines. This work presents a significant breakthrough in applying active inference to complex tasks, paving the way for a more thorough investigation of the framework's potential in robotic systems. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods yield unsatisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these complications, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by the unique properties of these data volumes by modeling both the spatial and value discrepancies through separate head networks within the encoder. Through BCAE, the data is represented using a reduced number of weight matrices and activations, resulting in improved compression ratios and reduced data manipulation time. The experimental outcomes verify that BCAE excels when data volumes have significant zero-value regions and minimal noise present. The study compares BCAE with various competing approaches such as Lightweight AutoEncoders (LAE) and Sparse Transformer (ST), demonstrating its superiority due to its ability to efficiently compress large 3D data volumes with minimal information loss while meeting the requirements of real-time data reduction. The efficacy of BCAE is validated by conducting thorough experiments using real-world data from the ATLAS TPC at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), achieving notable results with 3.29 bits per zero and significant state restoration time reductions of 41.69%. Calculations involving the orbital eccentricity of merging compact objects at the threshold of gravitational wave detection are crucial for predicting the properties of these objects based on observed signals. To achieve precise eccentricity estimates, we employed post-Newtonian theory for the final stages of the inspiral, which matched well with numerical simulations in phase space. Additionally, we found that higher-order harmonic interactions, often neglected in gravitational wave emissions, do have a significant impact. Consequently, we corrected previous findings and determined that for binary black holes inspiraling at 10 Hz when detected by Advanced LIGO, the residual eccentricity is approximately 0.003. Similarly, for neutron star-black hole inspirals, the residual eccentricity at 20 Hz is about 0.01. These results implied that a majority of neutron star-black hole mergers will yield distinct ringdown patterns following the merger. We based our analysis on a widely used theoretical framework but also compared it with an alternative model, which yielded comparable outcomes. Ultimately, we recommended utilizing more accurate models to characterize the properties of compact objects based on observed gravitational wave signals. Furthermore, we suggested that continued observations with Advanced LIGO and VIRGO could potentially detect eccentric gravitational waves from stellar-mass black hole coalescences at frequencies up to 20 Hz. Although less likely, it is not entirely ruled out. Lastly, we noted that 3rd generation gravitational wave detectors may be capable of detecting a broader range of eccentric events at higher frequencies, 40-100 Hz. Conversely, we found that these detectors may struggle to detect lower-frequency eccentric events, 0.1-2 Hz. To improve our understanding of gravitational wave detection capabilities, we developed and released a user-friendly tool, inspired by a previous resource, that allows researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of future detectors under diverse scenarios. In particular, we studied the behavior of gravitational wave detectors in an alternative gravitational wave model, which takes into account higher harmonic interactions and was shown to be a more accurate description of compact object inspirals at higher frequencies. Notably, this tool enabled us to investigate hypothetical detection capabilities for a more realistic scenario where the underlying physics of compact object inspirals is better understood. Specifically, we explored a scenario in which future detectors can efficiently detect and accurately characterize the properties of neutron star-black hole mergers at higher frequencies, 20-100 Hz. Conversely, we found that in a more realistic scenario where the underlying physics of these inspirals is better understood, 3rd generation gravitational wave detectors may struggle to detect and characterize these events at higher frequencies

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the electron beam allow for the tail to be at the threshold of gain while the leading bunch is in a regime of negative gain, effectively creating a self-sustaining amplifier. The implementation of this concept is envisioned to yield an extremely high-powered, fully coherent X-ray laser with unparalleled peak intensity. The central wavelength of the X-ray pulses can be finely controlled through a small change in the electron beam current, without compromising its high-coherence properties. This innovative approach is expected to significantly boost the performance of current and future hard X-ray laser facilities, ultimately enabling groundbreaking achievements in various fields such as atomic and molecular physics, condensed matter research, and medical applications. The achievable parameters include a 1 per second average output power of 100 GW, and an exceptionally high on-axis coherent peak power of 100 PW with the potential for a significantly higher peak power if implemented using a wedge-shaped electron beam as proposed here. The concept can also be applied for the mid-IR FEL amplifier to produce extremely high-powered femtosecond laser pulses in the 10 GW range. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties. By applying requirements engineering principles, the XAI field may develop a more user-centered approach, addressing the diverse needs of stakeholders in the explainable AI process. This includes prioritizing the most relevant requirements and incorporating the essential user considerations into the explainable AI system. Several user-related questions will be addressed such as who needs explanations, from which perspectives explanations should be provided, and how these perspectives can be bridged. With this paper, we aim to initiate a discussion on how requirements engineering can contribute to the improvement of explainable AI. A concrete example illustrates how the requirements engineering field can assist in addressing a critical XAI challenge, where the alignment of explanations with user goals is crucial. This alignment enables these users to grasp the purpose behind the provided explanations. With the aid of requirements engineering, the XAI field can ensure this alignment and develop explanations that are relevant and meaningful to users. In the absence of this alignment, users may reject explanations as mere technical deliberations without any connection to their needs and goals. Consequently, this paper concludes by emphasizing the necessity of integrating requirements engineering and XAI, with a direct connection between user-centered explainable AI and requirements engineering practices. With this integration, the development of explainable AI systems can become more focused on the diverse requirements and needs of stakeholders, thereby contributing to enhanced decision-making processes in both the XAI field and industry.

Characterizing colorectal polyps based on histological analysis is crucial for pinpointing areas with dysplastic properties and assessing their severity. This information is essential for guiding surgeons' decisions during polyp removal and subsequent follow-up treatments. Current gold standards for pathology review and adenoma grading rely on expert histopathologists' observations; however, this process is labor-intensive, and there is a scarcity of semi-automated systems that can efficiently support these tasks. Developed at the University of Genoa, Italy, is UniToPatho - a comprehensive dataset consisting of 93 High-Resolution Histological Stains paired with detailed Adenoma Grading Labels. This dataset caters to the needs of researchers by providing UniToPatho, designed to streamline and enhance current methods of histopathological analysis, ultimately contributing to the development of reliable semi-automatic tools for histopathologists. This research was facilitated by a collaboration between researchers from the University of Genoa and Valdani, S.p.A, a medical device manufacturer. This collaboration enabled researchers to establish a gold standard for defining areas with dysplastic properties and to create a dataset that is consistent with standard clinical protocols used to assess colorectal polyps. This research is significant, given that cancer detection through histopathological analysis is a proven and reliable method, and identifying areas with dysplastic properties is a vital component of this process. This research is a crucial step towards the development of a semi-automatic system for the precise identification of dysplastic areas in colorectal polyps and adenoma grading. Details about UniToPatho and related research, including code, dataset, and pre-trained models, can be found at https://unito-patho.github.io/. This resource provides information about the dataset, research papers, and the necessary code for recreating the semi-automatic classifier. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  The outcome is particularly beneficial for problems with lengthy circuit access requirements or expensive measurement costs.  Moreover, we observe that our approach facilitates reliable energy estimates with fewer circuit measurements, a crucial consideration when energy estimates are imperfect due to measurement noise.  The integration of the Bayesian method with QAOA exhibits potential to enhance the algorithm's classical portion, thereby empowering researchers to harness the potential of this quantum algorithm more effectively.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". A suitable Q-function can be effectively utilized for modeling, policy optimization, and reward estimation - these applications are theoretically proven. Moreover, we highlight the practical implications and experimental examples of the "small q-function" concept. Additionally, we introduce the notion of first arriving particle (FAP), which serves as a theoretical analysis tool for "small q-function" and enables the derivation of asymptotic properties. Using the FAP approach, we establish the asymptotic geometric interpolation between the Wang et al. (2020) model and traditional Q-learning. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applications and empirical examples of the theoretical results.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into distinctive vector signatures for vertebrae identification. To ensure robustness, this paper also proposes an anatomically-constrained optimization scheme to correct errors in vertebrae localization. The method was evaluated using two publicly available datasets, namely CentOS and Spine, and achieved impressive results, demonstrating the superiority of this approach over current state-of-the-art methods. The code for this research is openly available at https://github.com/PIK-DeepLearning/Vertebrae. Additionally, reconstructed spine models derived from this method's activation maps can be accessed at https://spine-rectifier.piik.ai. Both resources can support advanced medical applications and clinical treatments. The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from hydrodynamical models yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years. Furthermore, the transition to a full planetary disintegration is anticipated to occur before the end of the L-like stage, marking the final Protoplanetary disk phase, potentially rendering further transit observations during the L-like stage unfeasible. Ultimately, the predicted enhanced escapist tendencies of smaller, partially disintegrating planets pose significant challenges to detecting habitable-zone planets undergoing similar disintegration processes. Lastly, this research highlights the significance of observing exoplanets at various phases of planetary disintegration as well as different wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum. By capturing these various stages, astronomers can effectively appraise the timescales of planetary disintegration and evaluate their potential to discover habitable-zone exoplanets that may later become unstable. Time-domain transit observations combining spectral and photometric views may offer novel approaches to addressing these key questions. In the future, fellow astronomers are encouraged to contribute to this research by sharing their own observations of exoplanets, particularly those involving different wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum, to further this project. Additionally, utilizing newly developed, advanced telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Large Ultraviolet Optical Infrared Telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope, and the Giant Antenna, astronomers are poised to control the destiny of this area of study. By leveraging these powerful tools, it is anticipated that valuable insights regarding the stability of small, potentially habitable exoplanets will be gained. To that end

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a criterion for detecting codimension-two singularities that preserve the Milnor fibration and demonstrate its practical application in analyzing a critical space's irreducibility. Our findings offer a significant improvement over existing, more complex techniques. Additionally, we provide a flatness criterion for the critical space, which enhances known connectivity results and enables the computation of the Milnor fiber projective connection. These new findings deepen our understanding of the Milnor fibration and the geometry of the critical space. They also enable the computation of various topological invariants of the Milnor fiber and the vanishing locus of a holomorphic differential form on a complex projective variety. Lastly, we showcase a case study illustrating the utility of our theoretic outcomes via a concrete example originating from the study of rank-one torsion line bundles on K3 surfaces and elliptic surfaces. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. Therefore, it is Galileo's midlife shift towards philosophy, rather than a progressive development in scientific thinking, that deserves credit for popularizing the scientific method and promoting a philosophical understanding of science. This view is rooted in an in-depth analysis of Galileo's lesser-known works, as well as previously Translated works by prominent mathematicians. It is also supported by Nordmann's chronology, which documents the significant events in Galileo's life and the publication of various scientific works. Additionally, this response addresses several commonly raised objections to the hypothesis, as well as offering potential answers to yet another question raised by one of the objectors: what role did the Galileo affair play in shaping public perception of mathematics? It is suggested that a widespread misconception about Galileo's role may have contributed to an enduring misconception about the nature of mathematics. It is further proposed that mathematics is not merely a matter of following established rules but, rather, involves creative problem-solving and innovative thinking. Finally, it is observed that the view of mathematics as a purely empirical science lacks depth and is an oversimplification of the complex relationships between mathematical concepts, as demonstrated by the examples of continuum and infinitesimal. It is concluded that mathematics is, in fact, a self-consistent system of statements, as advocated for one hundred fifty years ago by Boole. It is also noted that a similar view, was independently expressed by Tarski, as well as by Frege, as well as by Russell. It is further pointed out that this view is not inherently contradictory to a semantic interpretation of mathematics. The increasing popularity of Tsallis' thermodynamic model, which deviates from the standard Boltzmann-Gas model, has been evident in recent years. This is, primarily, because of the'simple' generalization of Tsallis' formalism to relativistic systems. Although researchers have demonstrated the feasibility of applying Tsallis' formalism to the early universe using cosmological thermodynamic approaches, their findings are yet to be complemented by any alternative method. This work presents an approach to describe the ionization process based on Saha's formula, taking into account non-Gaussian behavior. We show that, under specific conditions, the number distribution of ions follows a Gaussian pattern, thereby validating the use of the Boltzmann-Gas model in cases where these conditions are met. This method can potentially serve as a means of testing Tsallis' formalism, thereby providing a tangible means of observing non-standard effects in the early universe. Additionally, we analyze the impact of discrete energy states on the early universe's thermodynamic properties, demonstrating how the application of Tsallis' formalism arises naturally from this consideration. These findings emphasize that only phenomena that emerge below their equilibrium thresholds can be attributed to non-standard effects. Conversely, the application of Tsallis' formalism to the early universe's thermodynamic properties, which is widely observed today, can be attributed to discrete energy states. These findings also underscore the necessity of investigating the discrete nature of energy states during thermodynamic analyses. Furthermore, we analyze radiation using a Fermi-Drude model, showing that non-standard effects emerge at high temperatures and densities, both of which characterize the early universe. However, we find that, in equilibrium situations, Tsallis' distribution reduces to the Boltzmann-Gas distribution. These findings are complemented by a thorough discussion and the presentation of a thesis for the 'physically acceptable' parameter value space. We also propose observing neutrino decays as a potential means of verifying non-standard effects in cosmology. However, we find that neutrino decays do not significantly influence the universe's evolution. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, poses significant modeling challenges. To address this, a novel approach combining the magnetohydrodynamics method with the particle-in-cell model has been developed. By embedding the particle-in-cell model within magnetohydrodynamics only in areas where reconnection is initiated, the computational cost associated with fully coupled methods can be substantially mitigated. The proposed method demonstrates promising results for studying the coalescence of magnetic islands, yielding outcomes comparable to fully coupled methods. Furthermore, the computational efficiency gains allow for the creation of detailed, self-consistent movies that provide valuable insights into the reconnection process. Based on the promising outcomes, this method can be a effective tool for accurately capturing the physical mechanisms underpinning reconnection in various astrophysical and laboratory settings. Additionally, the computational resource requirements can be tailored to balance accuracy and cost, making the method particularly suitable for studying phenomena at different spatial scales. The method's code is publicly available for research purposes. The research reported in this study was partially supported by the U.S. Department of Energy and by the European Research Council through the EXAFLIPO project. It was conducted using the JUQUEEN supercomputer at Jülich Supercomputing Center, operated by FZJ. The research involved participants from the Institute for Advanced Study and from the Institute for Computational Science and Technology. The authors would like to express their gratitude for the support received. To verify the efficacy of a novel numerical method for reconnection, a test case involving magnetic island coalescence has been utilized. The study commenced with an examination of the magnetic topology, particularly how a coherent structure connects with its mirror across a current sheet. The investigation revealed that when reconnection occurs, magnetic topology ceases to apply, thereby posing significant challenges for modeling. The test case relied on a suite of metrics to quantify the spatial integrity and temporal stability of reconnection, which can serve as crucial criteria for evaluating numerical methods. Furthermore, the study investigated the computational resources required to achieve stable reconnection, specifically how certain parameters behave over time. The test case was designed using a standard configuration and simulated employing two distinct numerical methods: a fully coupled approach and an newly developed method that combines magnetohydrodynamics with the particle-in-cell model. The results showed that both methods yield comparable outcomes, with notable differences in computational cost. The study offers an efficient approach for capturing the physical mechanisms underlying reconnection, thereby supporting research in astrophysics and laboratory settings. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.  As a practical demonstration of these principles, the course students worked in pairs to create Amanuensis - an intelligent assistant capable of writing relevant and useful code in short, descriptive phrases - using only publicly available resources and demonstrating key characteristics of human thought processes, including perception, memory, decision-making, and creativity.
